0.title: Amos: Let Justice Roll Down
0.overview:
Amos was a farmer, not a preacher. He was among the shepherds of Tekoa (1:1), a small town in the hills of Judah, and he also tended sycamore fig trees. He had no training as a prophet and belonged to no group of prophets. But one day the LORD took me from following the flock, and the LORD said to me, 'Go, prophesy to my people Israel' (7:15). So this countryman from the southern kingdom of Judah walked north into the wealthy kingdom of Israel and told it that God's judgment was coming.

He preached around 760 BC, in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake (1:1). It was a golden age for Israel. King Jeroboam II had won back lost territory, and Israel's borders reached further than they had for generations (2 Kgs 14:25). Money flowed. The rich built winter houses and summer houses, decorated their furniture with ivory, and held lavish parties. The shrines at Bethel and Gilgal were crowded with worshippers. Everyone felt that God was plainly blessing the nation.

But Amos saw what others overlooked. Behind the prosperity, the poor were being crushed. Judges took bribes. Merchants cheated with false weights. People lost their land and even their freedom over small debts; the rich would sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals (2:6). And the same people who oppressed the poor during the week filled the shrines on the holy days. Within about forty years of Amos's preaching, the Assyrians destroyed Samaria and carried Israel into exile (2 Kgs 17:6). The northern kingdom never returned.

The book falls into three main parts. Chapters 1-2 contain eight messages against the nations. Amos condemns Israel's neighbours one by one for their cruelty, then Judah, and finally, when his hearers are nodding in agreement, he turns on Israel itself. Chapters 3-6 are sermons against Israel, several opening with Hear this word (3:1; 4:1; 5:1) and including cries of Woe (5:18; 6:1). Chapters 7-9 contain five visions of judgment, interrupted by the story of the priest Amaziah trying to silence Amos. The book closes with a glorious promise of restoration (9:11-15).

Amos has a great deal to teach us. God rules all nations. He judges Syria, Philistia and Edom for their cruelty, even though they never had his written law. Privilege brings responsibility: You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities (3:2). God cares about the poor, and injustice against them is sin against him. Worship and justice belong together. God says of Israel's feasts, I hate, I despise them, and calls instead, let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream (5:21, 24). And God is the almighty Creator. Three times Amos breaks into hymns about the God who made the stars and commands the sea: the LORD, the God of hosts, is his name! (4:13; 5:8-9; 9:5-6).

Amos is sometimes read as if it were only about social justice, and sometimes its call to justice is quietly ignored by those who care only about personal faith. Amos will not let us do either. Israel's injustice was a symptom of a deeper problem: they had turned from God. And the answer was not first a political programme but a return to God himself: Seek me and live (5:4). Those who truly seek God will love what he loves, including justice for the weak.

Amos points us to Jesus Christ. The book opens with a lion's roar: The LORD roars from Zion (1:2), and Revelation names Jesus the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5). Amos prayed for Israel and twice judgment was held back (7:1-6), but Christ always lives to make intercession for his people (Heb 7:25). Amos warned that on the day of the LORD God would make the sun go down at noon and that there would be mourning like the mourning for an only son (8:9-10). When God's only Son died on the cross, there was darkness over the whole land from about noon until the ninth hour, while the sun's light failed (Luke 23:44-45). He bore the darkness of judgment so that his people might live in the light.

Above all, Amos ends with hope: In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen (9:11). At the council in Jerusalem, James quoted this promise to show that Gentiles coming to faith in Jesus, the Son of David, was what God had foretold (Acts 15:16-17). Christians understand the full fulfilment of these last verses in different ways. Many in the Reformed tradition see them fulfilled in Christ's reign and the gathering of the nations into his church, and completed in the new creation. Many dispensational Christians believe they also point to a future earthly kingdom and a restoration of Israel in the land. These notes explain both views where they arise. All agree that God's last word is not judgment but grace.

Amos still speaks with a lion's roar to comfortable, religious people. He asks us whether our worship is matched by the way we treat the poor, whether our success has made us complacent, and whether we truly want to hear God's word. But he also holds out God's great invitation: Seek the LORD and live (5:6). And he ends with a picture of God's people planted in a land of plenty, where they shall never again be uprooted (9:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The LORD Roars from Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: These are The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, given in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, two years before the earthquake (v. 1). His message opens with a terrifying sound: The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem, and the land withers before him (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: God is not silent. When he speaks in judgment, the whole land feels it.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.

Amos was not a professional prophet. He was among the shepherds of Tekoa, a small town in the hills of Judah about ten miles south of Jerusalem. (The ESV notes that the word may mean "sheep breeders", so he may have owned flocks rather than simply tending them.) Later he will tell a priest that he was also a dresser of sycamore figs (7:14). He was a working man from the southern kingdom of Judah, sent north to preach to the kingdom of Israel.

The date matters. Uzziah reigned in Judah and Jeroboam the son of Joash (usually called Jeroboam II) reigned in Israel. Amos preached around 760 BC. It was a time of peace and prosperity. Jeroboam had restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah (2 Kgs 14:25). The rich were building fine houses, the religious shrines were crowded, and people felt that God was plainly on their side. Into that confidence Amos brought a word of judgment. Within about forty years the Assyrians would destroy Israel's capital, Samaria, and carry the people away (2 Kgs 17:6).

Amos says he saw these words. God's message came to him as something he was shown, not something he invented. And it came two years before the earthquake. (The ESV notes it may mean "during two years".) This earthquake was so severe that people still spoke of it long afterward: Zechariah, writing centuries later, could say you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah (Zech 14:5). The shaking of the ground was a sign that the prophet's warnings were true.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said: "The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn, and the top of Carmel withers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: "The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn, and the top of Carmel withers."

This verse is the theme of the whole book. A shepherd knows exactly what a lion's roar means: danger is near and there is no time to waste (3:8). Now it is The LORD who roars. Joel uses the same words (Joel 3:16), but there the roar shelters God's people. Here it is turned against them.

Notice where the roar comes from: from Zion and from Jerusalem. The northern kingdom had broken away from Jerusalem and set up its own shrines at Bethel and Dan (1 Kgs 12:28-29). Amos reminds them that the true God still speaks from the place he chose, the city of David's royal line and of the temple. Their own shrines could not silence him.

The roar has an effect on the land. The pastures of the shepherds mourn, from the grazing lands in the south where Amos worked, to the top of Carmel, the fertile ridge on the northern coast, famous for its green woods. From one end of the land to the other, everything withers. When God speaks in judgment, creation itself dries up.

Christians should not picture God as a tame, soft voice that can be safely ignored. He is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5), and that title belongs to Jesus Christ. The same Lord who roars in judgment also laid down his life for his sheep. We must hear both.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three times comes the refrain: For three transgressions ... and for four, I will not revoke the punishment. Damascus crushed Gilead with iron threshing sledges (vv. 3-5). Gaza carried off whole communities to sell them to Edom (vv. 6-8). Tyre did the same and broke the covenant of brotherhood (vv. 9-10). Each time God promises, I will send a fire.
verseByVerse.theology: God holds even nations without his written law accountable for cruelty to other human beings.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have threshed Gilead with threshing sledges of iron. So I will send a fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad. I will break the gate-bar of Damascus, and cut off the inhabitants from the Valley of Aven, and him who holds the scepter from Beth-eden; and the people of Syria shall go into exile to Kir," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have threshed Gilead with threshing sledges of iron.

Now Amos begins a series of eight messages against the nations. Each opens with the same pattern: For three transgressions ... and for four. This was a common way of speaking in Hebrew poetry (compare Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand, Prov 30:18). It does not mean that the nation had sinned exactly four times. It means that sin had piled up past the full measure. Three would already be enough; four goes beyond it. God's patience had run its course. Yet usually only one sin is named, the one that shows the heart of the nation.

I will not revoke the punishment is literally "I will not turn it back" (as the ESV notes). The judgment is already on its way, like an arrow that has left the bow.

Damascus was the capital of Syria (also called Aram), Israel's northern neighbour and bitter enemy. Gilead was Israelite land east of the Jordan. Threshing sledges were heavy wooden boards with sharp pieces of iron or stone underneath, dragged over grain to break it apart. Damascus treated human beings like grain to be crushed. The book of Kings says the king of Syria had destroyed Israel's army and made them like the dust at threshing (2 Kgs 13:7).

So I will send a fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad.

Hazael seized the throne of Syria and waged brutal war against Israel. When Elisha foresaw it, he wept, telling Hazael, I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel (2 Kgs 8:12). Ben-hadad was the name of his son, who followed him on the throne. Fire means the burning of cities in war. The phrase I will send a fire will ring out again and again in these oracles. God is the one who sends it, even when he uses human armies to do it.

I will break the gate-bar of Damascus, and cut off the inhabitants from the Valley of Aven, and him who holds the scepter from Beth-eden; and the people of Syria shall go into exile to Kir," says the LORD.

The heavy bar that locked the city gate would be smashed. The Valley of Aven (the ESV notes "On" as another reading) and Beth-eden were probably places within the Syrian kingdom; their exact locations are uncertain. Him who holds the scepter means the ruler. And the people would be taken into exile to Kir. Later Amos says that God brought the Syrians from Kir (9:7). God would send them back where they came from, undoing their history. This happened within a few decades: The king of Assyria marched up against Damascus and took it, carrying its people captive to Kir (2 Kgs 16:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they carried into exile a whole people to deliver them up to Edom. So I will send a fire upon the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour her strongholds. I will cut off the inhabitants from Ashdod, and him who holds the scepter from Ashkelon; I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish," says the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they carried into exile a whole people to deliver them up to Edom.

Gaza was one of the chief cities of the Philistines, on the coast to the southwest of Judah. Its crime was slave trading on a massive scale. They carried into exile a whole people. This probably means they raided whole villages, taking everyone, men, women and children, and sold them to Edom, which could pass them on along the trade routes. Human beings were turned into merchandise. Joel brings a similar charge against the Philistines (Joel 3:4-6).

So I will send a fire upon the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour her strongholds.

I will cut off the inhabitants from Ashdod, and him who holds the scepter from Ashkelon; I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish," says the Lord GOD.

The judgment spreads from Gaza to the other Philistine cities: Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron. One of the five famous Philistine cities, Gath, is not named. It may already have been weakened, since Uzziah went to war against the Philistines and broke through the wall of Gath (2 Chr 26:6). The whole Philistine people is included, down to the remnant. What they did to others, sweeping away whole communities, will be done to them.

God did not give the Philistines the Ten Commandments. Yet he holds them responsible. Every person bears the image of God (Gen 9:6), and every conscience knows that selling people like cattle is wicked. Paul says that even those without the written law show that the work of the law is written on their hearts (Rom 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Tyre, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they delivered up a whole people to Edom, and did not remember the covenant of brotherhood. So I will send a fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour her strongholds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Tyre, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they delivered up a whole people to Edom, and did not remember the covenant of brotherhood.

Tyre was the great trading port of Phoenicia, on the coast north of Israel. Like Gaza, it trafficked in slaves, handing over a whole people to Edom. But there was an added sin. Tyre did not remember the covenant of brotherhood. This probably refers to the old friendship between Tyre and Israel. King Hiram of Tyre and Solomon made a treaty (1 Kgs 5:12), and Hiram even called Solomon my brother (1 Kgs 9:13). Tyre turned on its treaty partner and sold its people. Breaking a solemn promise is itself a sin God sees.

So I will send a fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour her strongholds."

Tyre was famous for its strength. Much of the city stood on an island just off the shore, and it held out against great empires. But no wall is high enough to keep out the fire God sends. Other prophets foretold its fall as well (Ezek 26), and in time the proud city was humbled.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, nursing endless rage against Israel (vv. 11-12). The Ammonites ripped open pregnant women in Gilead, that they might enlarge their border (v. 13). Fire will fall on Rabbah, and their king shall go into exile with his princes (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: No hatred is hidden from God, and no ambition justifies cruelty to the helpless.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because he pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger tore perpetually, and he kept his wrath forever. So I will send a fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the strongholds of Bozrah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because he pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger tore perpetually, and he kept his wrath forever.

Edom lay to the southeast of Judah. Its people descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob (Israel). That is why God speaks of his brother. Moses once greeted the king of Edom with the words Thus says your brother Israel (Num 20:14). But the relationship became one of long hatred.

Look at how the sin is described. Edom cast off all pity, deliberately shutting down every feeling of compassion. His anger tore perpetually, like a wild animal that keeps tearing at its prey. He kept his wrath forever, nursing a grudge from generation to generation. This is a portrait of bitterness. It begins in the heart and ends with the sword. Obadiah later condemned Edom for the same thing: Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you (Obad 10).

Bitterness is not only a national sin. Families, churches and friends can keep a grudge alive for years. Jesus teaches us to forgive from the heart, as we have been forgiven (Matt 18:35). The gospel is the only power that can end an old feud.

So I will send a fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the strongholds of Bozrah."

Teman and Bozrah were important places in Edom, standing for the whole nation. The fire of Edom's anger will be answered by the fire of God's judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of the Ammonites, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have ripped open pregnant women in Gilead, that they might enlarge their border. So I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour her strongholds, with shouting on the day of battle, with a tempest in the day of the whirlwind; and their king shall go into exile, he and his princes together," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of the Ammonites, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have ripped open pregnant women in Gilead, that they might enlarge their border.

The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan, next to Israel's territory in Gilead. Their crime is horrifying. In war they ripped open pregnant women, killing mothers and unborn children together. Why? That they might enlarge their border. They wanted more land, and they were willing to wipe out the next generation of Gilead to get it.

God names the unborn as victims. Their lives mattered to him. Greed for land, wealth or power can make people willing to destroy the most defenceless of all. God sees, and God judges it. Every society that treats the weak and the unborn as obstacles to its own ambitions stands under this word.

So I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour her strongholds, with shouting on the day of battle, with a tempest in the day of the whirlwind;

Rabbah was the capital of Ammon (the site of modern Amman in Jordan). The judgment comes with the shouting of soldiers storming the city, and it sweeps in like a tempest and the whirlwind. Human armies attack, but behind them stands the power of God, as irresistible as a storm.

and their king shall go into exile, he and his princes together," says the LORD.

The leaders who planned the atrocities will be carried away. (The ESV notes that princes may mean "officials".) Those who drove others out to enlarge their borders will themselves be driven out of their land.

Picture Amos preaching this in Israel. The crowd would have loved it. Syria, Philistia, Tyre, Edom and Ammon were all Israel's enemies, and God was condemning each one. But Amos is drawing a circle around Israel, nation by nation, and the circle is closing. In the next chapter he will reach Judah, and then Israel itself. Before we cheer at God's judgment on others, we must remember that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Rom 3:23).

1.title: The Lion Roars
1.overview:
Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa in Judah, received God's word concerning Israel during the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, two years before a great earthquake. His message begins with the LORD roaring from Zion, so that the pastures mourn and Carmel withers (vv. 1-2).

Then come the oracles against the nations, each opening, "For three transgressions ... and for four, I will not revoke the punishment". Damascus threshed Gilead with iron sledges; fire will fall on the house of Hazael and the Syrians will go into exile to Kir (vv. 3-5). Gaza carried off whole communities to sell to Edom; Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron will perish with it (vv. 6-8). Tyre sold whole communities to Edom and broke the covenant of brotherhood (vv. 9-10).

Edom pursued his brother with the sword, cast off all pity and kept his wrath forever; fire will fall on Teman and Bozrah (vv. 11-12). The Ammonites ripped open pregnant women in Gilead to enlarge their border; fire will fall on Rabbah amid the shouting of battle, and their king and princes will go into exile (vv. 13-15).
1.theology:
God speaks, and his word of judgment is like a lion's roar that no one can ignore (v. 2; 3:8; Joel 3:16; Rev 5:5).

God rules over all nations, not Israel only, and he is patient, but his patience has an end (vv. 3, 6, 9, 11, 13; Acts 17:30-31).

Even nations without the written law are accountable to God, because his law is written on the conscience and every person bears his image (vv. 3-15; Rom 1:18-20; 2:14-15; Gen 9:6).

God hates cruelty, trafficking, broken promises, lasting hatred and violence against the helpless, including the unborn (vv. 3, 6, 9, 11, 13).

God repays sin in kind: those who drove others from their homes are themselves driven into exile (vv. 5, 15; Obad 15).

Judgment on others is a warning to ourselves, for all have sinned (vv. 3-15; 2:4-6; Rom 2:1; 3:23).
1.examples:
A shepherd from the south sent to preach in the palaces of the north.

A lion's roar that withers the pastures and dries the top of Carmel.

Iron sledges dragged over people as if they were grain.

Whole villages marched away and sold on the trade routes.

A brother who cast off all pity and kept his anger forever.

Unborn children killed for a few more miles of land.

A crowd cheering as the circle of judgment closes around them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom (v. 1). Fire will fall on Kerioth, and Moab will die amid the noise of battle, its ruler and princes with it (vv. 2-3).
verseByVerse.theology: God defends the dignity of every human being, even in death, and even an enemy of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because he burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom. So I will send a fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the strongholds of Kerioth, and Moab shall die amid uproar, amid shouting and the sound of the trumpet; I will cut off the ruler from its midst, and will kill all its princes with him," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because he burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom.

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Its crime was not against Israel at all, but against Edom. Moab burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom, perhaps digging up a dead king and burning his remains to powder. We do not know when this happened, since it is not recorded elsewhere. In the ancient world this was the ultimate insult, an attempt to destroy a man even after death.

This matters. Edom was no friend of Israel, and chapter 1 has just condemned Edom. Yet God defends the dignity of Edom's king. God's justice is not favouritism toward his own side. Every human being, friend or enemy, living or dead, is made in his image and belongs to him.

So I will send a fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the strongholds of Kerioth, and Moab shall die amid uproar, amid shouting and the sound of the trumpet;

I will cut off the ruler from its midst, and will kill all its princes with him," says the LORD.

Kerioth was a town of Moab. Moab will fall in the noise of war, and its ruler and his princes (the ESV notes "officials") will fall with it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the circle reaches Amos's own people. Judah has rejected the law of the LORD and followed the lies of their fathers (v. 4). So I will send a fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the strongholds of Jerusalem (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Having God's word brings no protection to those who reject it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Judah, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have rejected the law of the LORD, and have not kept his statutes, but their lies have led them astray, those after which their fathers walked. So I will send a fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the strongholds of Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Judah, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have rejected the law of the LORD, and have not kept his statutes, but their lies have led them astray, those after which their fathers walked.

Imagine the crowd in Israel. They had nodded along as Amos condemned Syria, Philistia, Tyre, Edom, Ammon and Moab. Now he turns to Judah, Israel's southern rival. That too would have pleased them. But notice the change in the charge. The other nations were judged for cruelty against the conscience. Judah is judged for rejecting the law of the LORD. Judah had God's written word, and more is expected from those who have it. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (Luke 12:48).

Their lies probably means false gods and false teaching, the empty idols that had deceived their fathers too. Sin had become a family tradition.

So I will send a fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the strongholds of Jerusalem."

Even Jerusalem, the city of God's temple, is not safe. About 170 years later the Babylonians burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem (2 Kgs 25:9). Being near God's things is no substitute for obeying God's word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Finally Israel itself: they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals, trample the poor, defile a girl and drink at the altar on the backs of the poor (vv. 6-8). Yet God destroyed their enemies, brought them out of Egypt, and gave them prophets and Nazirites (vv. 9-11). They silenced the prophets (v. 12), so no strength or speed will save them in the day of judgment (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The greater God's kindness to a people, the greater their guilt when they despise it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals— those who trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the afflicted; a man and his father go in to the same girl, so that my holy name is profaned; they lay themselves down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge, and in the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals—

Now the trap springs. The circle of judgment has closed around Israel, the very people listening. It is like the prophet Nathan telling David a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's lamb, and then saying, You are the man! (2 Sam 12:7). And Israel's charge sheet is by far the longest.

Israel's sins were not war crimes against foreigners, but injustice against their own poor neighbours. They sell the righteous for silver: innocent people were sold into slavery for debt, or judges were bribed to condemn them. The needy for a pair of sandals: a poor man could lose his freedom over a debt as small as the price of a pair of shoes.

those who trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the afflicted; a man and his father go in to the same girl, so that my holy name is profaned;

The rich trample the poor into the ground and push aside anyone who tries to get justice. Then comes sexual sin: a man and his father go in to the same girl. We are not told who she was. She may have been a servant girl in the household, or a prostitute at a pagan shrine. Either way, father and son use the same young woman, and God says his holy name is profaned, because his people bear his name.

they lay themselves down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge, and in the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined.

A poor man who borrowed could give his cloak as security. God's law said, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down, for that is his only covering (Exod 22:26-27). But the lenders kept the cloaks and lay on them at religious feasts beside the altar. They bought wine with fines squeezed out of the poor and drank it in the house of their God. They were worshipping God on the backs of the people he told them to protect. Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker (Prov 14:31).

These were not pagans. They went to worship, gave offerings and sang at the feasts. That is what makes the passage so searching for churchgoers today. A Christian can attend faithfully and still exploit people during the week: paying workers unfairly, lending on crushing terms, cutting corners on a poor tenant, or simply looking away from a neighbour in need. John asks, if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him? (1 John 3:17). God reads our worship by the way we treat the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars and who was as strong as the oaks; I destroyed his fruit above and his roots beneath. Also it was I who brought you up out of the land of Egypt and led you forty years in the wilderness, to possess the land of the Amorite. And I raised up some of your sons for prophets, and some of your young men for Nazirites. Is it not indeed so, O people of Israel?" declares the LORD. "But you made the Nazirites drink wine, and commanded the prophets, saying, 'You shall not prophesy.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Yet it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars and who was as strong as the oaks; I destroyed his fruit above and his roots beneath.

Also it was I who brought you up out of the land of Egypt and led you forty years in the wilderness, to possess the land of the Amorite.

God reminds Israel of his kindness. The Amorite stands for the peoples of Canaan, who seemed like giants to the spies (Num 13:32-33). God cut them down like a tree, fruit above and ... roots beneath. He rescued Israel from Egypt, carried them through the wilderness and gave them the land. The emphasis falls on I: everything they had was his gift.

And I raised up some of your sons for prophets, and some of your young men for Nazirites. Is it not indeed so, O people of Israel?" declares the LORD.

"But you made the Nazirites drink wine, and commanded the prophets, saying, 'You shall not prophesy.'

God also gave spiritual gifts. Prophets brought his word. Nazirites were people who took a special vow of devotion to God, which included refusing all wine (Num 6:3). They were living reminders of holiness. Israel pressured the Nazirites to break their vows and told the prophets to be quiet. Amos himself would soon hear it: never again prophesy at Bethel (7:13). Later Stephen asked, Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? (Acts 7:52). The same pattern reached its climax when God sent his Son, and they crucified him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I will press you down in your place, as a cart full of sheaves presses down. Flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not retain his strength, nor shall the mighty save his life; he who handles the bow shall not stand, and he who is swift of foot shall not save himself, nor shall he who rides the horse save his life; and he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, I will press you down in your place, as a cart full of sheaves presses down.

The judgment is pictured as a cart loaded with harvested grain, pressing down with crushing weight. Israel had pressed down the poor. Now God will press them down.

Flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not retain his strength, nor shall the mighty save his life;

he who handles the bow shall not stand, and he who is swift of foot shall not save himself, nor shall he who rides the horse save his life;

and he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day," declares the LORD.

Every kind of strength is listed: speed, power, the archer, the runner, the horseman, the bravest soldier. None of it will help. The bravest will run away naked, throwing off armour and clothes to escape. Israel trusted in its military success under Jeroboam, but no strength can stand against God.

There is only one way to escape the judgment of God, and it is not by running. It is by taking refuge in the One who bore it. Jesus came to proclaim good news to the poor and to set at liberty those who are oppressed (Luke 4:18), and though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Cor 8:9). Those who have received such grace cannot go on crushing the poor. How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? (Heb 2:3).

2.title: You Are the Man
2.overview:
The oracles against the nations continue. Moab burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom; fire will fall on Kerioth, and Moab's ruler and princes will die amid the shouts of battle (vv. 1-3). Then Judah: they rejected the law of the LORD and were led astray by the lies their fathers followed, so fire will devour the strongholds of Jerusalem (vv. 4-5).

Finally the circle closes on Israel. They sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, trample the poor into the dust, turn aside the afflicted, profane God's name as father and son go in to the same girl, and lie beside the altars on garments taken in pledge, drinking the wine of those they have fined (vv. 6-8).

Yet God destroyed the mighty Amorite before them, brought them up from Egypt, led them forty years in the wilderness, and raised up prophets and Nazirites among them. But they made the Nazirites drink wine and told the prophets not to prophesy (vv. 9-12). So God will press them down like a loaded cart; the swift, the strong, the archer and the horseman will not escape, and the bravest will flee away naked in that day (vv. 13-16).
2.theology:
God defends the dignity of every person, even an enemy, even in death (v. 1; Gen 9:6).

Those who have God's word are judged by it, and privilege increases responsibility (vv. 4-5; Luke 12:48; Rom 2:1).

Injustice against the poor is sin against God, and religion practised on the backs of the poor is hateful to him (vv. 6-8; Exod 22:26-27; Prov 14:31; Jas 2:6).

God's past kindness makes ingratitude and rebellion more serious, not less (vv. 9-11).

Silencing God's messengers is a long pattern of rebellion that reached its climax in the rejection of Christ (v. 12; 7:12-13; Acts 7:52; Matt 23:37).

No human strength can escape God's judgment; the only refuge is Christ, who became poor for our sake (vv. 13-16; Luke 4:18; 2 Cor 8:9; Heb 2:3).
2.examples:
An enemy king's bones burned to powder, and God taking his side.

A crowd applauding judgment until the prophet reaches their own city.

A man sold into slavery for the price of a pair of shoes.

A poor man's only cloak spread out at a worship feast.

A Nazirite handed a cup of wine and told to break his vow.

The bravest soldier running from the battle without his clothes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks to the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt (v. 1): You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities (v. 2). A string of questions shows that every effect has a cause (vv. 3-6). God does nothing without revealing it to his prophets (v. 7), and The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy? (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Being chosen by God is not a shield against judgment but a reason for greater accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O people of Israel, against the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O people of Israel, against the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt:

The oracles against the nations are over, and Amos now turns to Israel alone. Chapters 3-6 contain his sermons against the northern kingdom, and three of them begin with the command Hear this word (3:1; 4:1; 5:1). God addresses the whole family he rescued from Egypt, which includes Judah as well as Israel. He reminds them who they are: a family he redeemed.

"You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.

This is a startling sentence. God obviously knows about every nation; chapters 1-2 have just shown that. But in the Bible, for God to know someone often means to choose them and bind himself to them in love. God said to Jeremiah, Before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jer 1:5). Out of all the nations, God set his love on Israel, not because they were great, but simply because he loved them (Deut 7:7-8).

We might expect the next word to be "therefore I will protect you". Instead it is therefore I will punish you. Israel thought being chosen meant they were safe no matter how they lived. Amos says the opposite. Privilege brings responsibility. The closer the relationship, the more serious the betrayal.

This speaks directly to the church. Peter writes, it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God (1 Pet 4:17). For a Christian, God's discipline is not a sign that he has abandoned us, but a sign that he loves us as his children: the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Heb 12:6). Grace is never a licence to sin. Those who truly know they are loved by God will not treat that love lightly.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet? Does a lion roar in the forest, when he has no prey? Does a young lion cry out from his den, if he has taken nothing? Does a bird fall in a snare on the earth, when there is no trap for it? Does a snare spring up from the ground, when it has taken nothing? Is a trumpet blown in a city, and the people are not afraid? Does disaster come to a city, unless the LORD has done it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Do two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet?

Does a lion roar in the forest, when he has no prey? Does a young lion cry out from his den, if he has taken nothing?

Does a bird fall in a snare on the earth, when there is no trap for it? Does a snare spring up from the ground, when it has taken nothing?

Amos asks a series of simple questions, the kind a shepherd from the countryside would ask. Every answer is obviously "No". Two people do not meet in the wilderness by accident. A lion roars when it has caught its prey. A bird does not fall to the ground unless there is a trap. A trap does not spring shut unless something has triggered it. The point is plain: nothing happens without a cause. Every effect has something behind it.

These questions are leading somewhere. Israel wanted to know why Amos was preaching such a harsh message. Why this strange shepherd from Judah? Why these warnings? The questions answer: because something has caused it.

Is a trumpet blown in a city, and the people are not afraid? Does disaster come to a city, unless the LORD has done it?

Now the questions come closer to home. When the watchman blows the trumpet on the city wall, everyone trembles, because an enemy is coming. And when disaster comes, who is behind it? The LORD has done it. The disasters that fall on Israel will not be accidents or mere politics. God will be at work in them.

Christians have wrestled with this truth. Some prefer to say that God only allows disasters. The Reformed tradition, following passages like this, teaches that God rules over all things, including calamity: I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things (Isa 45:7). Yet God is never the author of sin, and those who do evil are fully responsible for it. The comfort in this is great. No disaster is meaningless, and nothing is outside the hand of a God who is wise and good. Nothing can snatch his people out of Christ's hand (John 10:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "For the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets. The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets.

Here is the chain of cause and effect reaching its point. God does not bring judgment secretly or without warning. He tells his servants the prophets first. A secret is something shared only with those close to you. Long before, God said about his friend Abraham, Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do (Gen 18:17). The very fact that Amos is preaching is a mercy. God warns before he strikes, so that people may turn.

We have received something greater. God has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:2), and Jesus told his disciples, all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:15). Scripture is God's open counsel. No one will be able to say on the last day that he did not warn us.

The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?"

This verse brings together the lion of 1:2 and the questions of verses 3-6. When a lion roars nearby, everyone is afraid; it is the natural response. In the same way, when God speaks, the prophet cannot keep silent. Amos did not choose this ministry for himself. He is a man under compulsion. Jeremiah described the same thing as a burning fire shut up in my bones (Jer 20:9), and the apostles said, we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard (Acts 4:20).

There are two responses in the verse: fear and prophecy. The listener should fear, and the preacher must speak. Every faithful pastor feels the weight of this. Paul said, Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! (1 Cor 9:16). And every hearer should tremble, not with a panic that runs from God, but with the reverent fear that runs to him for mercy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pagan nations are summoned to look at the oppression in Samaria, where they store up violence and robbery in their strongholds (vv. 9-10). An enemy will surround the land (v. 11), and Israel will be "rescued" like scraps from a lion's mouth (v. 12). God will punish the altars of Bethel and strike down the winter houses, summer houses and houses of ivory (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: False worship and luxury built on injustice will both fall on the day God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: Proclaim to the strongholds in Ashdod and to the strongholds in the land of Egypt, and say, "Assemble yourselves on the mountains of Samaria, and see the great tumults within her, and the oppressed in her midst." "They do not know how to do right," declares the LORD, "those who store up violence and robbery in their strongholds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Proclaim to the strongholds in Ashdod and to the strongholds in the land of Egypt, and say, "Assemble yourselves on the mountains of Samaria, and see the great tumults within her, and the oppressed in her midst."

God calls for witnesses, as in a courtroom. And he chooses surprising ones: Ashdod, a Philistine city, and Egypt, Israel's ancient oppressor. These pagan nations are invited to sit on the hills around Samaria, Israel's capital, and look down into the city. What will they see? Great tumults, meaning disorder and violence, and the oppressed. Even the pagans will be shocked. The very nation God had rescued from slavery in Egypt now makes slaves of its own people.

"They do not know how to do right," declares the LORD, "those who store up violence and robbery in their strongholds."

Samaria's leaders had lost even the ability to do right. Sin practised long enough dulls the conscience until it no longer feels wrong. Their great houses were full of treasure, but God saw it for what it was: violence and robbery, wealth taken from the poor and stored away. James says the same to the rich who oppress: their corrosion will be evidence against you (Jas 5:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "An adversary shall surround the land and bring down your defenses from you, and your strongholds shall be plundered." Thus says the LORD: "As the shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear, so shall the people of Israel who dwell in Samaria be rescued, with the corner of a couch and part of a bed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "An adversary shall surround the land and bring down your defenses from you, and your strongholds shall be plundered."

The punishment fits the crime. The strongholds where they stored up plunder will themselves be plundered. An enemy will surround the land. (The ESV notes the Hebrew is abrupt: "An adversary, one who surrounds the land—he shall bring down".) Amos does not name the enemy, but history does. Assyria came, besieged Samaria for three years, and carried Israel into exile (2 Kgs 17:5-6).

Thus says the LORD: "As the shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear, so shall the people of Israel who dwell in Samaria be rescued, with the corner of a couch and part of a bed.

Amos draws on his own work. Under God's law, if a wild animal killed a sheep in a shepherd's care, he had to bring back what was left as evidence that he had not stolen it: If it is torn by beasts, let him bring it as evidence (Exod 22:13). So a shepherd might pull two legs, or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth. That is not a rescue. It is proof that the sheep is dead.

Israel will be "rescued" in the same way. All that will be left of the rich in Samaria is the corner of a couch and part of a bed (the ESV notes that the meaning of the word translated part is uncertain). The furniture they lounged on (6:4) will be the only evidence that they were ever there. Those who hope for a small remnant to survive in comfort will find nothing but scraps.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, and testify against the house of Jacob," declares the Lord GOD, the God of hosts, "that on the day I punish Israel for his transgressions, I will punish the altars of Bethel, and the horns of the altar shall be cut off and fall to the ground. I will strike the winter house along with the summer house, and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall come to an end," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hear, and testify against the house of Jacob," declares the Lord GOD, the God of hosts,

The witnesses are told to testify. God calls himself the God of hosts, the commander of the armies of heaven. Israel's army could not protect them from him.

"that on the day I punish Israel for his transgressions, I will punish the altars of Bethel, and the horns of the altar shall be cut off and fall to the ground.

Bethel was the chief shrine of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf (1 Kgs 12:28-29). It was the heart of Israel's religion. Altars had horns, projections at each corner, and a person fleeing for his life could take hold of them to seek mercy (1 Kgs 1:50). If the horns are cut off, there is no place of refuge left. False religion cannot save anyone on the day of judgment. Years later, King Josiah pulled down the altar at Bethel and burned it (2 Kgs 23:15).

Only one altar truly offers refuge. Christ's sacrifice is the place where sinners can take hold and find mercy.

I will strike the winter house along with the summer house, and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall come to an end," declares the LORD.

The wealthy had two homes: a winter house in a warmer place and a summer house in a cooler one (Jer 36:22 mentions a king's winter house). Some had houses of ivory, decorated with carved ivory panels. King Ahab had built an ivory house in Samaria (1 Kgs 22:39), and archaeologists digging there have found many pieces of carved ivory. The great houses (the ESV notes "many houses") will come to an end.

God is not against homes or beautiful things. But these houses were built with wealth taken from the poor, and their owners trusted in them. Jesus warned, Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matt 6:19, 21). Everything we build without God will come to an end. Only what is built on Christ will last. And we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Cor 5:10).

3.title: You Only Have I Known
3.overview:
God speaks against the whole family he brought out of Egypt: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" (vv. 1-2). A series of questions shows that every effect has a cause: two do not walk together without meeting, a lion does not roar without prey, a snare does not spring without a catch, and disaster does not come to a city unless the LORD has done it (vv. 3-6). God does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets; the lion has roared, and the prophet cannot keep silent (vv. 7-8).

Ashdod and Egypt are summoned to look on the tumults and oppression in Samaria, whose people store up violence and robbery in their strongholds (vv. 9-10). An adversary will surround the land and plunder those strongholds, and Israel will be rescued only as a shepherd rescues two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth, with nothing left but the corner of a couch and part of a bed (vv. 11-12).

The nations are called to testify: on the day God punishes Israel he will punish the altars of Bethel and cut off the horns of the altar, and he will strike the winter house and summer house, and the houses of ivory and great houses will come to an end (vv. 13-15).
3.theology:
God's choice of his people is an act of free love, and it brings greater accountability, not immunity from judgment (vv. 1-2; Deut 7:6-8; Luke 12:48; 1 Pet 4:17; Heb 12:6).

God rules over all events, including calamity, yet he is never the author of sin (v. 6; Isa 45:7; Lam 3:37-38).

God warns before he judges, revealing his purposes through his prophets and finally through his Son (v. 7; Gen 18:17; Heb 1:1-2; John 15:15).

When God speaks, the right response is fear, and his messengers cannot keep silent (v. 8; Jer 20:9; Acts 4:20; 1 Cor 9:16).

Wealth gained by oppression is stored-up guilt, and it will not last (vv. 9-10, 15; Jas 5:1-3; Matt 6:19-21).

False worship offers no refuge; the only true place of mercy is the sacrifice of Christ (v. 14; 1 Kgs 1:50; 2 Cor 5:10).
3.examples:
A chosen family told that its privilege makes its guilt heavier.

A lion's roar that means the prey is already caught.

A trap that does not spring unless something has set it off.

A prophet who cannot keep God's word shut up inside him.

Egypt and the Philistines invited to sit on the hills and watch Samaria's injustice.

A shepherd holding up two legs and a piece of an ear.

An altar with its horns cut off and no refuge left.

Ivory panels and summer houses buried under the ruins.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Cows of Bashan and Busy Worshippers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wealthy women of Samaria, who oppress the poor, who crush the needy, will be dragged away with hooks (vv. 1-3). With biting irony God invites Israel to keep going to its shrines: Come to Bethel, and transgress, for so you love to do (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Luxury built on oppression and worship that loves to be seen are both hateful to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear this word, you cows of Bashan, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor, who crush the needy, who say to your husbands, 'Bring, that we may drink!' The Lord GOD has sworn by his holiness that, behold, the days are coming upon you, when they shall take you away with hooks, even the last of you with fishhooks. And you shall go out through the breaches, each one straight ahead; and you shall be cast out into Harmon," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hear this word, you cows of Bashan, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor, who crush the needy, who say to your husbands, 'Bring, that we may drink!'

Bashan was rich grazing land east of the Jordan, famous for its sleek, well-fed cattle (Deut 32:14). Amos calls the wealthy women of Samaria cows of Bashan. It was a shocking insult from a man who worked with animals. These women were pampered and fat on the good life. They may never have struck a poor person themselves, but their demands drove the system: Bring, that we may drink! Their husbands squeezed the poor to pay for their wives' parties. God counts them among those who oppress the poor.

This is a warning for anyone who lives comfortably. We may not personally cheat anyone, yet we can happily enjoy the fruits of injustice without asking where they came from. Scripture calls the rich not to be haughty nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim 6:17).

The Lord GOD has sworn by his holiness that, behold, the days are coming upon you, when they shall take you away with hooks, even the last of you with fishhooks.

And you shall go out through the breaches, each one straight ahead; and you shall be cast out into Harmon," declares the LORD.

God swears by his holiness, the strongest oath possible, because there is nothing higher. The women who lived like fattened cattle will be dragged away like fish on hooks. When the enemy breaks down the city walls, they will be marched out single file through the gaps (the breaches), each one straight ahead. Harmon is unknown to us; it may have been a place on the road into exile.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come to Bethel, and transgress; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression; bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days; offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving of that which is leavened, and proclaim freewill offerings, publish them; for so you love to do, O people of Israel!" declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Come to Bethel, and transgress; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression; bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days;

This is heavy sarcasm. A priest would call, "Come to Bethel and worship!" Amos says, Come to Bethel, and transgress. Bethel and Gilgal were Israel's great shrines, packed with worshippers. But every visit only added to their sin. Go on, says God, bring sacrifices every morning and tithes every three days. The more zealous they were in religion while oppressing the poor, the more guilty they became.

offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving of that which is leavened, and proclaim freewill offerings, publish them; for so you love to do, O people of Israel!" declares the Lord GOD.

The heart of the problem is in the last words: for so you love to do. They loved religion. They loved to proclaim and publish their generous offerings so that everyone knew. But they did not love God, and they did not love their neighbours. Jesus described the same thing: hypocrites who love to stand and pray ... that they may be seen by others (Matt 6:5). It is possible to be very religious and very far from God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Yet You Did Not Return to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sent famine, drought, blight and locusts, plague and war, and a disaster like Sodom's, and after each one comes the refrain: yet you did not return to me (vv. 6-11). So prepare to meet your God, O Israel! (v. 12). He is the Creator who forms the mountains and creates the wind; the LORD, the God of hosts, is his name! (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's hard providences are calls to repentance, and those who refuse them must at last meet God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "I gave you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in all your places, yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD. "I also withheld the rain from you when there were yet three months to the harvest; I would send rain on one city, and send no rain on another city; one field would have rain, and the field on which it did not rain would wither; so two or three cities would wander to another city to drink water, and would not be satisfied; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I gave you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in all your places, yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.

Now God reviews a series of disasters he had already sent. Cleanness of teeth is a grim way of saying that there was no food to chew. These were not random events. God says, I gave you. His law had warned that if Israel broke the covenant, he would send famine, drought, disease and defeat (Deut 28:22-24). Each disaster was a warning shot, meant to turn them back to him.

Five times the same sad refrain sounds: yet you did not return to me (vv. 6, 8, 9, 10, 11). It is the voice of a father calling a wayward child home, again and again.

"I also withheld the rain from you when there were yet three months to the harvest; I would send rain on one city, and send no rain on another city; one field would have rain, and the field on which it did not rain would wither;

so two or three cities would wander to another city to drink water, and would not be satisfied; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.

The rain failed at the worst possible time, three months before harvest, when crops needed it most. And it fell in a strange pattern: one town got rain, the next did not. That was a sign that this was not mere weather. God was showing his hand. Thirsty people staggered from town to town looking for water. Yet they still did not come to the One who could give them living water.

verseByVerse.quote: "I struck you with blight and mildew; your many gardens and your vineyards, your fig trees and your olive trees the locust devoured; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD. "I sent among you a pestilence after the manner of Egypt; I killed your young men with the sword, and carried away your horses, and I made the stench of your camp go up into your nostrils; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD. "I overthrew some of you, as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were as a brand plucked out of the burning; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I struck you with blight and mildew; your many gardens and your vineyards, your fig trees and your olive trees the locust devoured; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.

"I sent among you a pestilence after the manner of Egypt; I killed your young men with the sword, and carried away your horses, and I made the stench of your camp go up into your nostrils; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.

Crops rotted with blight and mildew, and locusts ate the rest. Then came plague after the manner of Egypt. The plagues God once sent on Pharaoh were now falling on his own people, because they had become like Egypt. War killed their young men and captured their horses (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads "along with the captivity of your horses"). The smell of unburied bodies filled the camp.

"I overthrew some of you, as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were as a brand plucked out of the burning; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.

Some disaster, perhaps an earthquake or a great fire, was so terrible that it could only be compared to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24-25). Israel survived it only barely, like a brand plucked out of the burning, that is, a burning stick snatched from the fire before it was consumed (as the ESV notes). They had been rescued at the last moment. Surely now they would turn back to God? Yet you did not return to me.

Suffering does not automatically make people repent. It can soften the heart, or it can harden it. Revelation describes people who lived through terrible plagues and still did not repent of the works of their hands (Rev 9:20). God's kindness and his discipline are both meant to lead you to repentance (Rom 2:4). When hardship comes, the right question is not only "Why me?" but "Lord, what are you calling me to turn from?"

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus I will do to you, O Israel; because I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel!" For behold, he who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought, who makes the morning darkness, and treads on the heights of the earth— the LORD, the God of hosts, is his name!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore thus I will do to you, O Israel; because I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel!"

After five warnings ignored, God no longer sends another warning. He comes himself. Prepare to meet your God. Notice that God does not say exactly what he will do. The silence is more frightening than any description. Israel had been meeting at Bethel and Gilgal for worship. Now they will meet God in judgment.

These words are true for every person. It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27). How can anyone be prepared to meet a holy God? Not by religious activity like Israel's, but by coming to God through Jesus Christ, who met God's judgment in our place. The prodigal son prepared to meet his father by coming home in repentance, and found his father running to embrace him (Luke 15:20). Behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2).

For behold, he who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought, who makes the morning darkness, and treads on the heights of the earth— the LORD, the God of hosts, is his name!

Amos breaks into a hymn of praise, and a similar hymn will return in 5:8-9 and 9:5-6. Who is this God Israel must meet? He forms the mountains and creates the wind, the solid and the invisible alike. He declares to man what is his thought. This may mean that God reveals his own plans to people (3:7), or that he shows people their own hidden thoughts, since he knows them all (Ps 139:2). He makes the morning darkness, able to turn dawn into night. He treads on the heights of the earth, like a giant striding over the mountains.

Israel had shrunk God down to a local god who could be kept happy with sacrifices at Bethel. Amos lifts their eyes to the Creator of all things, and the meeting with him cannot be escaped. But the same almighty God is the one who in Christ became a man, walked our roads and calls sinners to himself.

4.title: Prepare to Meet Your God
4.overview:
Amos addresses the wealthy women of Samaria as cows of Bashan, who oppress the poor, crush the needy and demand drink from their husbands. God has sworn by his holiness that they will be taken away with hooks and marched out through the breaches in the walls (vv. 1-3). With bitter irony he invites Israel to Bethel and Gilgal to multiply transgression with daily sacrifices, frequent tithes and publicised offerings, for so they love to do (vv. 4-5).

God lists the disciplines he had already sent: famine, drought that fell on one city and not another, blight, mildew and locusts, pestilence like Egypt's and defeat in war, and an overthrow like Sodom and Gomorrah from which they were rescued like a brand from the fire. After each comes the refrain, "yet you did not return to me" (vv. 6-11).

Therefore Israel must prepare to meet its God (v. 12), the one who forms the mountains, creates the wind, declares his thought to man, makes the morning darkness and treads on the heights of the earth, whose name is the LORD, the God of hosts (v. 13).
4.theology:
Enjoying luxury built on the oppression of the poor makes us guilty of that oppression (vv. 1-3; 1 Tim 6:17; Jas 5:1-3).

Religious zeal that loves display and ignores obedience multiplies sin rather than removing it (vv. 4-5; Matt 6:5).

God rules over famine, drought, disease and disaster, and uses them to call his people to return (vv. 6-11; Deut 28:22-24; Lev 26:23-24).

Suffering does not by itself produce repentance; hearts can harden under discipline (vv. 6-11; Rom 2:4; Rev 9:20-21; Jer 5:3).

Every person must meet God, and the only preparation is repentance and faith in Christ (v. 12; Heb 9:27; 2 Cor 6:2; Luke 15:17-20).

The God we must meet is the almighty Creator, whose name is the LORD of hosts (v. 13; Mic 1:3; Ps 139:1-4; Heb 10:31).
4.examples:
Pampered women calling for another drink while the poor go hungry.

Worshippers announcing their generous offerings for all to hear.

Rain falling on one town and passing over the next.

A burning stick pulled from the fire just in time.

Five warnings, and five times the same sad refrain.

A people told to prepare, not for another warning, but for God himself.
