verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amos sings a funeral song over Israel: Fallen, no more to rise, is the virgin Israel (vv. 1-3). Yet God still calls, Seek me and live; but do not seek Bethel (vv. 4-5). Seek the LORD and live, before his fire breaks out on those who turn justice to wormwood (vv. 6-7). He is the Maker of the Pleiades and Orion, who brings destruction on the strong (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Even as judgment approaches, God holds out life to all who will seek him, not religious places but himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this word that I take up over you in lamentation, O house of Israel: "Fallen, no more to rise, is the virgin Israel; forsaken on her land, with none to raise her up." For thus says the Lord GOD: "The city that went out a thousand shall have a hundred left, and that which went out a hundred shall have ten left to the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this word that I take up over you in lamentation, O house of Israel:

A lamentation was a funeral song, sung over the dead. Imagine walking into a busy, prosperous city and singing a funeral song over people who were eating, trading and worshipping around you. That is what Amos did. Israel was alive and wealthy, but in God's sight the nation was already dead.

"Fallen, no more to rise, is the virgin Israel; forsaken on her land, with none to raise her up."

Israel is pictured as the virgin Israel, a young woman who should have had her whole life ahead of her, now struck down and lying alone on the ground. No more to rise, and none to raise her up: no ally, no army, no idol will help. The northern kingdom did fall to Assyria and never rose again as a nation.

For thus says the Lord GOD: "The city that went out a thousand shall have a hundred left, and that which went out a hundred shall have ten left to the house of Israel."

Towns sent out their fighting men in units. A city that sent out a thousand soldiers would see only a hundred come home. A village that sent out a hundred would see ten. Nine out of every ten would be lost. Behind the numbers are real families waiting at the gate for sons who never return.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD to the house of Israel: "Seek me and live; but do not seek Bethel, and do not enter into Gilgal or cross over to Beersheba; for Gilgal shall surely go into exile, and Bethel shall come to nothing." Seek the LORD and live, lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and it devour, with none to quench it for Bethel, O you who turn justice to wormwood and cast down righteousness to the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD to the house of Israel: "Seek me and live;

Into the funeral song comes an astonishing invitation. The sentence of death has been pronounced, and yet God says, Seek me and live. This is the gospel in a single sentence. God does not delight in judgment. As long as the door is open, he calls. Isaiah says the same: Seek the LORD while he may be found (Isa 55:6).

but do not seek Bethel, and do not enter into Gilgal or cross over to Beersheba; for Gilgal shall surely go into exile, and Bethel shall come to nothing."

Israel thought it was seeking God. People crowded into the famous holy places. Bethel was where God had met Jacob, Gilgal was where Israel first camped in the promised land, and Beersheba, in the far south of Judah, was where Abraham called there on the name of the LORD (Gen 21:33). Pilgrims even crossed the border to visit it.

But God says, do not seek the places; seek me. A shrine with a great history cannot save anyone. Gilgal shall surely go into exile, and Bethel shall come to nothing. The places people trusted in would be destroyed. It is possible to love the church building, the tradition, the famous preacher or the religious experience, and not seek God himself. Jesus is not one holy place among many. He is the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6).

Seek the LORD and live, lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and it devour, with none to quench it for Bethel,

The invitation is repeated, with a warning. The house of Joseph means the northern kingdom, whose leading tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, descended from Joseph. If they will not seek God, his judgment will break out like fire, and no priest at Bethel will be able to put it out.

O you who turn justice to wormwood and cast down righteousness to the earth!

Wormwood is a very bitter plant (the ESV notes it may be "bitter fruit"). Justice should be sweet and life-giving to the poor. Israel's courts had turned it into something bitter. Righteousness was thrown to the ground and trampled. Seeking God and doing justice cannot be separated.

verseByVerse.quote: He who made the Pleiades and Orion, and turns deep darkness into the morning and darkens the day into night, who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out on the surface of the earth, the LORD is his name; who makes destruction flash forth against the strong, so that destruction comes upon the fortress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who made the Pleiades and Orion, and turns deep darkness into the morning and darkens the day into night, who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out on the surface of the earth, the LORD is his name;

Once again Amos breaks into a hymn (compare 4:13). The Pleiades, a small cluster of stars, and Orion, the great hunter in the night sky, were familiar to every shepherd who watched his flock at night. God made them (Job 9:9). He controls day and night. He calls for the waters of the sea, drawing them up as clouds and pouring them out as rain, or perhaps as a flood. The LORD is his name.

Why put a hymn about the stars in the middle of a sermon about justice? Because the God who orders the heavens is the God who sees the courts of Samaria. He is not a small god to be kept in a shrine. And the same power that turns deep darkness into the morning can turn a lost life into a new day.

who makes destruction flash forth against the strong, so that destruction comes upon the fortress.

The Creator is also the Judge. The powerful thought their wealth and walls made them safe. God's judgment strikes like lightning, suddenly and without warning, on the strong and on the fortress.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel hates anyone who speaks the truth in court (v. 10). Those who trample the poor will not live in their stone houses (v. 11). God knows their bribes and injustice, and it is an evil time (vv. 12-13). Seek good, and not evil, that you may live; Hate evil, and love good, and establish justice in the gate (vv. 14-15). Otherwise there will be wailing everywhere, for I will pass through your midst (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: True seeking of God shows itself in loving what he loves and doing justice.

verseByVerse.quote: They hate him who reproves in the gate, and they abhor him who speaks the truth. Therefore because you trample on the poor and you exact taxes of grain from him, you have built houses of hewn stone, but you shall not dwell in them; you have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine. For I know how many are your transgressions and how great are your sins— you who afflict the righteous, who take a bribe, and turn aside the needy in the gate. Therefore he who is prudent will keep silent in such a time, for it is an evil time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They hate him who reproves in the gate, and they abhor him who speaks the truth.

In ancient Israel the town gate was the place of the law court. The elders sat there to hear cases and settle disputes (Ruth 4:1). Him who reproves in the gate was the honest witness or judge who spoke up for what was right. Israel's leaders hated such people. Anyone who told the truth about their corruption was an enemy. People who love sin always hate the one who exposes it, and Amos himself would soon feel that hatred (7:10-13).

Therefore because you trample on the poor and you exact taxes of grain from him, you have built houses of hewn stone, but you shall not dwell in them; you have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine.

The rich trample on the poor (the ESV notes it may be "you tax") and take their grain. With the profits they built houses of hewn stone, expensive homes of cut stone rather than the ordinary mud brick. They planted fine vineyards. But they would never enjoy them. God's law had warned: You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it. You shall plant a vineyard, but you shall not enjoy its fruit (Deut 28:30). What is gained by injustice will be lost.

For I know how many are your transgressions and how great are your sins— you who afflict the righteous, who take a bribe, and turn aside the needy in the gate.

The corrupt officials may have thought no one knew about the bribes. God says, I know. He knows how many sins there are, and how serious. The righteous man is harassed, the judge takes a bribe, and the poor man who comes to court for help is sent away without a hearing.

Therefore he who is prudent will keep silent in such a time, for it is an evil time.

This verse is not easy. Most take it as a sad description of the times: things had become so corrupt that sensible people kept their mouths shut, because speaking up was useless or even dangerous. Others think it means that when judgment falls, the wise will be silent before God. Either way, it is not a command for believers to stay quiet about injustice. Amos himself refused to keep silent. It shows how dark a society has become when honest people are afraid to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: Seek good, and not evil, that you may live; and so the LORD, the God of hosts, will be with you, as you have said. Hate evil, and love good, and establish justice in the gate; it may be that the LORD, the God of hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seek good, and not evil, that you may live; and so the LORD, the God of hosts, will be with you, as you have said.

The call to seek and live comes a third time (vv. 4, 6, 14). Now it becomes practical: Seek good, and not evil. To seek God is to seek what God loves. As you have said: Israel liked to say that God was with them. They sang it at their feasts. Amos says that God truly will be with them, but only if they turn from evil. God's presence is not a slogan for people who ignore his will.

Hate evil, and love good, and establish justice in the gate; it may be that the LORD, the God of hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.

Repentance is more than feeling sorry. It reaches the emotions: Hate evil, and love good. And it reaches public life: establish justice in the gate, the courts where the poor had been denied a hearing. True faith changes both the heart and the way we treat others.

It may be that the LORD ... will be gracious. Amos does not say that God owes them mercy. Joel uses similar words: Who knows whether he will not turn and relent (Joel 2:14). Grace is always a gift, never something we can demand. And notice the remnant of Joseph. Amos already sees that judgment will come, but a remnant may yet be spared. This hope of a remnant will grow into the promise at the end of the book (9:8-15).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the Lord: "In all the squares there shall be wailing, and in all the streets they shall say, 'Alas! Alas!' They shall call the farmers to mourning and to wailing those who are skilled in lamentation, and in all vineyards there shall be wailing, for I will pass through your midst," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the Lord: "In all the squares there shall be wailing, and in all the streets they shall say, 'Alas! Alas!' They shall call the farmers to mourning and to wailing those who are skilled in lamentation,

The funeral song of verse 1 becomes a national funeral. Wailing fills the squares and the streets. At funerals people hired professional mourners, those who are skilled in lamentation. There would be so many dead that even the farmers would be called from the fields to help with the mourning.

and in all vineyards there shall be wailing, for I will pass through your midst," says the LORD.

Vineyards were places of joy at harvest time, full of singing. Now they will be filled with wailing. Why? For I will pass through your midst. These words recall the night of the Passover, when God said, I will pass through the land of Egypt that night (Exod 12:12). Then he passed through Egypt to judge it and spared his people. Now Israel has become like Egypt, and God will pass through them in judgment. There is no protection in belonging to God's people outwardly if the heart is far from him. Our only shelter is the blood of Christ, the true Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The Day of the LORD and the Feasts God Hates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD! It will be darkness, and not light (vv. 18-20). God says, I hate, I despise your feasts (vv. 21-23). But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream (v. 24). Their worship is mixed with idols, so God will send them into exile beyond Damascus (vv. 25-27).
verseByVerse.theology: God refuses worship that is separated from justice, and those who presume on his day will find it dark.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD! Why would you have the day of the LORD? It is darkness, and not light, as if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him, or went into the house and leaned his hand against the wall, and a serpent bit him. Is not the day of the LORD darkness, and not light, and gloom with no brightness in it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD! Why would you have the day of the LORD? It is darkness, and not light,

The day of the LORD was a popular hope in Israel. People looked forward to the day when God would step in, defeat Israel's enemies and bless his people. They longed for it. Amos says, Woe to you. They had forgotten that God's day brings judgment on all sin, including theirs. For people living in rebellion, that day will be darkness, and not light.

Many people still assume that God is on their side and that the last day will go well for them, without ever facing their own sin. That is a dangerous assumption.

as if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him, or went into the house and leaned his hand against the wall, and a serpent bit him.

Amos paints a picture any shepherd could understand. A man escapes a lion, only to run into a bear. He escapes the bear, gets safely home, leans against the wall to catch his breath, and a snake hidden in a crack bit him. There is no escape. Just when he feels safe, he is struck. So it will be on the day of the LORD for those who are not right with God.

Is not the day of the LORD darkness, and not light, and gloom with no brightness in it?

The repetition drives it home: darkness, gloom, no brightness. Yet there is good news here too. When Christ hung on the cross, there was darkness over all the land (Matt 27:45). He entered that darkness of God's judgment for his people. That is why Paul can tell believers, you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief (1 Thess 5:4). For those in Christ, the day of the Lord is the day of his appearing, a day of light.

verseByVerse.quote: "I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies. Even though you offer me your burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them; and the peace offerings of your fattened animals, I will not look upon them. Take away from me the noise of your songs; to the melody of your harps I will not listen. But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies.

These are strong words. I hate, I despise. And he is speaking about your feasts and your solemn assemblies, the religious festivals Israel celebrated so eagerly. Notice the word your. They were no longer God's feasts. They had become Israel's own.

Even though you offer me your burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them; and the peace offerings of your fattened animals, I will not look upon them.

Take away from me the noise of your songs; to the melody of your harps I will not listen.

God names every kind of offering: burnt offerings, grain offerings and peace offerings of the best, fattened animals. He will not accept them or even look upon them. Their music, with all its skill and beauty, is to him only noise. God is not against sacrifice or music; he commanded both. But worship offered by people who crush the poor on Monday is not worship to him. Samuel had said long before, to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22).

But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.

Here is what God wants instead. In Israel, many streambeds were full of water in the rainy season but completely dry in the summer. Israel's justice was like that: it appeared for the festival and vanished in daily life. God wants justice that flows like waters, rolling down like a river in flood, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream that never dries up, all year round, in the courts and in the marketplace. This verse has often been quoted by people fighting for justice in modern times, and rightly so.

Jesus pressed the same point on the religious leaders of his day. They tithed even their garden herbs, but neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness (Matt 23:23). Christian worship is not only what happens on Sunday. Paul calls us to present our whole lives as a living sacrifice (Rom 12:1). And justice that truly flows like a river can only come from hearts that have been made new by the grace of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? You shall take up Sikkuth your king, and Kiyyun your star-god—your images that you made for yourselves, and I will send you into exile beyond Damascus," says the LORD, whose name is the God of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?

God looks back to the wilderness. The question may expect the answer "No", or at least "Not mainly". During those forty years, the heart of Israel's relationship with God was not a busy system of sacrifices but trust and obedience. Jeremiah makes a similar point: the command God gave was Obey my voice, and I will be your God (Jer 7:23). Others read the question as pointing to Israel's mixed worship even in the wilderness, when they offered sacrifices and still turned to idols. Both readings lead to the same conclusion: God has always wanted hearts, not just rituals.

You shall take up Sikkuth your king, and Kiyyun your star-god—your images that you made for yourselves,

Sikkuth and Kiyyun were probably star-gods worshipped in Mesopotamia. Israel had begun to mix the worship of the LORD with the worship of the heavenly bodies. The ESV reads the verse as a prediction: when they go into exile, they will carry their idols with them, gods that cannot even carry themselves. Other translations read it as a description of what Israel had already done.

Stephen quoted these verses in his speech before he was stoned: You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan (Acts 7:43). His wording is different mainly because he was quoting the Greek translation of the Old Testament that was widely used in his day. The point is the same: God's people had turned to false gods again and again, and they rejected God's messengers, just as they were now rejecting Christ.

and I will send you into exile beyond Damascus," says the LORD, whose name is the God of hosts.

Beyond Damascus meant further away than Israel's familiar northern enemy, all the way to Assyria. (Stephen says beyond Babylon, applying the words to the later exile of Judah as well.) The God whose feasts they turned into their own, and whose law they ignored, would send them far from the land. It is a sobering end to a chapter that began with an invitation: Seek me and live. That invitation still stands today for all who come to God through Christ.

5.title: Let Justice Roll Down
5.overview:
Amos takes up a funeral lament over Israel: fallen, no more to rise, the virgin Israel lies forsaken, and her cities will be left with a tenth of their fighting men (vv. 1-3). Yet God calls, "Seek me and live", not Bethel, Gilgal or Beersheba, which will go into exile and come to nothing. Seek the LORD and live, lest he break out like fire on those who turn justice to wormwood (vv. 4-7). He made the Pleiades and Orion, turns darkness into morning, pours out the sea on the earth and flashes destruction on the strong (vv. 8-9).

Israel hates those who speak the truth in the gate. Because they trample the poor and tax their grain, they will not live in their houses of hewn stone or drink the wine of their vineyards. God knows their bribes and their injustice to the needy; it is an evil time, when the prudent keep silent (vv. 10-13). "Seek good, and not evil, that you may live"; hate evil, love good and establish justice in the gate, and it may be that God will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph (vv. 14-15). Otherwise wailing will fill the squares and vineyards, for God will pass through their midst (vv. 16-17).

Woe to those who desire the day of the LORD: it is darkness and not light, like a man who flees a lion and meets a bear, or leans on a wall and is bitten by a serpent (vv. 18-20). God hates and despises their feasts, offerings and songs; instead, "let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (vv. 21-24). Since the wilderness their worship has been mixed with idols, and they will carry Sikkuth and Kiyyun into exile beyond Damascus (vv. 25-27).
5.theology:
God sees the death of a sinful nation before it happens and mourns over it (vv. 1-3, 16-17).

Even in judgment God freely offers life to all who seek him, and seeking him means seeking him, not religious places or traditions (vv. 4-6, 14; Isa 55:6-7; John 14:6).

The Creator of the stars is the Judge of every courtroom and marketplace (vv. 8-9; 4:13; Job 9:9).

True repentance changes both what we love and how we act in public life (vv. 14-15; Mic 6:8).

The day of the LORD is darkness for all who presume on God's favour while living in sin; Christ entered that darkness so that believers are children of light (vv. 18-20; Matt 27:45; 1 Thess 5:4-5).

God rejects worship that is separated from justice and mercy (vv. 21-24; Isa 1:11-17; 1 Sam 15:22; Matt 23:23; Rom 12:1).

Mixing the worship of God with other gods leads to exile (vv. 25-27; Acts 7:42-43).
5.examples:
A funeral song sung in the middle of a busy, prosperous city.

Pilgrims crowding famous shrines while ignoring the God they were built for.

A judge's bribe taken in the gate where the poor wait in vain.

A stone house built with stolen grain and never lived in.

A man who escapes a lion and a bear and is bitten by a snake at home.

Fine music that sounds like noise in heaven.

A dry streambed in summer, and a river that never stops flowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Woe to Those at Ease
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria, who push away the thought of disaster (vv. 1-3). They lounge on beds of ivory, feast, sing and drink wine in bowls, but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph! (vv. 4-6). They will be the first of those who go into exile (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Comfort that makes us careless of God and blind to others' ruin is under God's woe.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the first of the nations, to whom the house of Israel comes! Pass over to Calneh, and see, and from there go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. Are you better than these kingdoms? Or is their territory greater than your territory, O you who put far away the day of disaster and bring near the seat of violence?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the first of the nations, to whom the house of Israel comes!

A woe was a cry of grief, the kind of word spoken at a funeral (compare 5:18). This woe falls on the leaders of both kingdoms: those at ease in Zion (Jerusalem) and those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria. Their sin was complacency. They were rich, powerful and sure that nothing could touch them. They thought of themselves as the notable men of the first of the nations, the elite of the greatest nation, to whom ordinary people came for help and favours.

Complacency is a quiet, respectable sin. It does not look like wickedness. It looks like success. Jesus told of a rich man who said to himself, relax, eat, drink, be merry, the very night his life was required of him (Luke 12:19-20). The church in Laodicea said, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing (Rev 3:17).

Pass over to Calneh, and see, and from there go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. Are you better than these kingdoms? Or is their territory greater than your territory,

Amos sends them on a tour. Calneh and Hamath were important cities to the north, and Gath was a Philistine city to the southwest. Gath had already been captured and broken (2 Kgs 12:17; 2 Chr 26:6). Were those kingdoms weaker or smaller than Israel? No. If proud and powerful cities like these could fall, why did Israel think it could not?

O you who put far away the day of disaster and bring near the seat of violence?

They pushed the day of disaster far out of their minds, and at the same time they brought violence closer by their injustice. They refused to think about judgment while they were hastening it. While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them (1 Thess 5:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory and stretch themselves out on their couches, and eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the stall, who sing idle songs to the sound of the harp and like David invent for themselves instruments of music, who drink wine in bowls and anoint themselves with the finest oils, but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph! Therefore they shall now be the first of those who go into exile, and the revelry of those who stretch themselves out shall pass away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory and stretch themselves out on their couches, and eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the stall,

Amos describes a party of the rich. They recline on beds of ivory, couches inlaid with carved ivory (compare 3:15). They stretch themselves out, lazy and overfed. Most people in Israel ate meat only on special occasions. These people ate the choicest lambs and calves fattened in the stall, as everyday food.

who sing idle songs to the sound of the harp and like David invent for themselves instruments of music,

They make up idle songs, empty entertainment, and think of themselves as great musicians like David. But David made instruments to offer praises to the LORD (1 Chr 23:5). These people made music for themselves.

who drink wine in bowls and anoint themselves with the finest oils, but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph!

Cups were not enough; they drank wine in bowls. They rubbed themselves with the finest oils, the expensive perfumes of the day. Now comes the heart of the charge: they are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph. The nation (Joseph, the northern tribes) was rotting from within. The poor were being crushed and judgment was coming. And they felt nothing.

God does not condemn feasting, music or perfume in themselves. Scripture is full of feasts and songs. The sin is enjoying good things while being indifferent to the suffering around us and the spiritual ruin of God's people. Nehemiah heard of Jerusalem's ruin and sat down and wept and mourned for days (Neh 1:4). Jesus saw the city and wept over it (Luke 19:41). The test for us is simple: what breaks our hearts?

Therefore they shall now be the first of those who go into exile, and the revelry of those who stretch themselves out shall pass away."

A grim irony: they thought they were the first of the nations (v. 1), so they will be the first to go into exile. The party will end. Pride goes before destruction (Prov 16:18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — I Abhor the Pride of Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God swears by himself: I abhor the pride of Jacob (v. 8). Death will fill the houses, and survivors will be afraid even to speak God's name (vv. 9-11). Israel has done something as absurd as plowing rock, turning justice into poison and boasting in its own strength (vv. 12-13). God will raise up a nation to oppress them from one end of the land to the other (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: God opposes the proud, and every victory we credit to our own strength will be taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD has sworn by himself, declares the LORD, the God of hosts: "I abhor the pride of Jacob and hate his strongholds, and I will deliver up the city and all that is in it." And if ten men remain in one house, they shall die. And when one's relative, the one who anoints him for burial, shall take him up to bring the bones out of the house, and shall say to him who is in the innermost parts of the house, "Is there still anyone with you?" he shall say, "No"; and he shall say, "Silence! We must not mention the name of the LORD." For behold, the LORD commands, and the great house shall be struck down into fragments, and the little house into bits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord GOD has sworn by himself, declares the LORD, the God of hosts: "I abhor the pride of Jacob and hate his strongholds, and I will deliver up the city and all that is in it."

God has sworn by himself, since he had no one greater by whom to swear (Heb 6:13). The judgment is certain. I abhor the pride of Jacob. The things Israel was proudest of, its wealth, its fortresses and its success, God hates, because they had taken his place in their hearts. The city, Samaria, will be handed over to the enemy with everything in it. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5:5).

And if ten men remain in one house, they shall die.

And when one's relative, the one who anoints him for burial, shall take him up to bring the bones out of the house, and shall say to him who is in the innermost parts of the house, "Is there still anyone with you?" he shall say, "No"; and he shall say, "Silence! We must not mention the name of the LORD."

A terrible scene, probably during the siege, when plague and death fill the city. Even if ten men survive the fighting and shelter in one house, they will die. A relative comes to take out the bodies for burial and calls to someone hiding in the back room, Is there still anyone with you? The answer is No. Then comes a chilling word: Silence! We must not mention the name of the LORD. The survivor is afraid that even speaking God's name might draw his attention and bring more judgment. People who once used God's name lightly at their feasts are now terrified of it.

For behold, the LORD commands, and the great house shall be struck down into fragments, and the little house into bits.

No one is spared: the great house of the rich and the little house of the ordinary family. It happens because the LORD commands.

verseByVerse.quote: Do horses run on rocks? Does one plow there with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood — you who rejoice in Lo-debar, who say, "Have we not by our own strength captured Karnaim for ourselves?" "For behold, I will raise up against you a nation, O house of Israel," declares the LORD, the God of hosts; "and they shall oppress you from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do horses run on rocks? Does one plow there with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood—

Amos asks two ridiculous questions. Would anyone gallop horses over jagged rocks? Would anyone plow rock with oxen? (The ESV notes the second question may be read as plowing "the sea".) Of course not. It would ruin the animals and achieve nothing. Yet Israel has done something just as absurd and unnatural. They took justice, which should heal a society, and turned it into poison. They took righteousness, which should bear sweet fruit, and turned it into wormwood, a bitter plant (the ESV notes "bitter fruit"). Injustice is not only wicked. It is foolishness that goes against the grain of the world God made.

you who rejoice in Lo-debar, who say, "Have we not by our own strength captured Karnaim for ourselves?"

Lo-debar and Karnaim were towns east of the Jordan, probably won back in Jeroboam's successful wars. Israel celebrated these victories. But Amos makes a play on the names. As the ESV notes, Lo-debar means "nothing", and Karnaim means "horns", a symbol of strength. So they are celebrating a victory over Nothing, and boasting that by our own strength they took "Horns". Their proud achievements amount to nothing.

The deeper problem is the words by our own strength. God had warned Israel never to say, My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth (Deut 8:17-18). Paul asks us, What do you have that you did not receive? (1 Cor 4:7). Every success in business, ministry or family is a gift of God's grace. The only safe boast is in knowing the Lord (Jer 9:24).

"For behold, I will raise up against you a nation, O house of Israel," declares the LORD, the God of hosts; "and they shall oppress you from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah."

The nation is not named, but it was Assyria. And notice the boundaries: from Lebo-hamath in the far north to the Brook of the Arabah in the south. These are the same northern and southern limits Jeroboam had won when he restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah (2 Kgs 14:25). All the territory Israel boasted of winning by its own strength would be overrun. What we build in pride, God can take away. What we receive from his hand in humility, we hold as his gift.

6.title: At Ease in Zion
6.overview:
Woe to the complacent leaders at ease in Zion and secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the first of the nations. Let them look at Calneh, Hamath and Gath: are they better than those kingdoms? They put far away the day of disaster while bringing near the seat of violence (vv. 1-3).

Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory, eat the choicest lambs and calves, sing idle songs and invent instruments like David, drink wine in bowls and anoint themselves with the finest oils, but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph. They will be the first to go into exile, and their revelry will pass away (vv. 4-7).

The Lord GOD has sworn by himself that he abhors the pride of Jacob and will deliver up the city. If ten men remain in one house, they will die, and the one who carries out the bones will hush any mention of the LORD's name; great house and little house will be shattered (vv. 8-11). Israel has done something as absurd as running horses on rocks, turning justice into poison and righteousness into wormwood, rejoicing in Lo-debar and boasting of taking Karnaim by their own strength. So God will raise up a nation to oppress them from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah (vv. 12-14).
6.theology:
Complacency and a false sense of security are sins that God will judge (vv. 1-3; Luke 12:19-20; Rev 3:17; 1 Thess 5:3).

Enjoying God's good gifts while indifferent to the ruin of others and of God's people is under his woe (vv. 4-6; Neh 1:4; Rom 12:15; Luke 19:41).

God hates pride and opposes the proud (vv. 7-8; Prov 16:18; 1 Pet 5:5).

Injustice is not only wicked but foolish, contrary to the order of God's world (v. 12).

Every success is God's gift, and boasting in our own strength invites his judgment (vv. 13-14; Deut 8:17-18; 1 Cor 4:7; Jer 9:23-24).
6.examples:
Leaders lounging on ivory couches while the nation rots.

Wine drunk from bowls because cups are too small.

A party with music and perfume, and not one tear for the ruin outside.

A survivor hushing anyone who mentions the name of God.

A farmer trying to plow a rock with oxen.

A victory celebration over a town called Nothing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows Amos locusts devouring the land, and Amos prays, O Lord GOD, please forgive! How can Jacob stand? He is so small! The LORD relented (vv. 1-3). Then a judgment by fire, and again Amos pleads and God relents (vv. 4-6). Then the Lord stands beside a wall with a plumb line in his hand: I am setting a plumb line in the midst of my people Israel; I will never again pass by them (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: God hears the prayers of those who stand in the gap, yet there comes a point when he measures his people by his standard and judgment must fall.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, he was forming locusts when the latter growth was just beginning to sprout, and behold, it was the latter growth after the king's mowings. When they had finished eating the grass of the land, I said, "O Lord GOD, please forgive! How can Jacob stand? He is so small!" The LORD relented concerning this: "It shall not be," said the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, he was forming locusts when the latter growth was just beginning to sprout, and behold, it was the latter growth after the king's mowings.

Chapters 7-9 contain five visions. The first four follow a pattern, and the first three are here. God showed Amos what he was about to do. In the first vision God is forming locusts, like a potter shaping clay. The timing is terrible. The first cutting of grass, the king's mowings, was probably the king's share, taken as a tax. What grew back afterwards, the latter growth, was what the ordinary people and their animals would live on. If locusts ate that, there would be nothing left until the next year. It would mean famine.

When they had finished eating the grass of the land, I said, "O Lord GOD, please forgive! How can Jacob stand? He is so small!"

Amos is not a cold, harsh preacher who enjoys announcing judgment. When he sees what is coming, he immediately prays for the very people who reject him. Please forgive! Notice what he does not say. He does not argue that Israel deserves mercy. He appeals to their weakness: How can Jacob stand? He is so small! Israel thought it was strong and important (6:1, 13). Amos sees it as a small, helpless child before the power of God.

The LORD relented concerning this: "It shall not be," said the LORD.

God answered the prayer. The LORD relented. The plague did not come. Scripture tells us several times that God relented in response to prayer or repentance, as when Moses pleaded for Israel after the golden calf (Exod 32:14).

How can an unchanging God relent? Some Christians conclude that God truly changes his plans in response to what happens. The Reformed tradition, with most of the church through history, holds that God does not change his eternal purpose (Num 23:19; Mal 3:6). Instead, he has ordained that prayer is one of the means by which he carries out his purposes. The warning was real, the prayer was real and the answer was real. God meant to spare Israel for a time, and he meant to do it through the prayer of his prophet. That should make us pray more, not less. The prayer of a righteous person has great power (Jas 5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, the Lord GOD was calling for a judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep and was eating up the land. Then I said, "O Lord GOD, please cease! How can Jacob stand? He is so small!" The LORD relented concerning this: "This also shall not be," said the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, the Lord GOD was calling for a judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep and was eating up the land.

The second vision is even more terrible. God calls for a judgment by fire. It is so hot that it dries up the great deep, the vast waters under the earth that fed springs and rivers, and then starts eating up the land. This may picture a burning drought so severe that nothing survives.

Then I said, "O Lord GOD, please cease! How can Jacob stand? He is so small!"

The LORD relented concerning this: "This also shall not be," said the Lord GOD.

Again Amos intercedes. This time he does not even say "forgive". He simply begs God to stop: please cease! And again God relents. Twice judgment is held back because one man stood between God and the people. God once searched for someone to stand in the breach before me for the land and found none (Ezek 22:30). Here he found one.

Amos points us to a greater Intercessor. Jesus Christ always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through him (Heb 7:25). Amos could only delay judgment. Christ took the judgment on himself, so that his people are spared forever. And every Christian is called to pray for their family, church and nation with the same compassion Amos showed.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what he showed me: behold, the Lord was standing beside a wall built with a plumb line, with a plumb line in his hand. And the LORD said to me, "Amos, what do you see?" And I said, "A plumb line." Then the Lord said, "Behold, I am setting a plumb line in the midst of my people Israel; I will never again pass by them; the high places of Isaac shall be made desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste, and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what he showed me: behold, the Lord was standing beside a wall built with a plumb line, with a plumb line in his hand.

The third vision is quieter but more final. A plumb line is a weight hanging on a string. Builders used it to check whether a wall was perfectly upright. Gravity never lies; the string always hangs straight. The Lord stands beside a wall built with a plumb line, a wall that was built straight in the beginning. Israel had been built true by God, but now he comes to test whether it is still straight.

And the LORD said to me, "Amos, what do you see?" And I said, "A plumb line." Then the Lord said, "Behold, I am setting a plumb line in the midst of my people Israel; I will never again pass by them;

God asks, Amos, what do you see? Now he explains. He is setting his plumb line in the midst of my people Israel. He will measure them by his own standard, not by their opinion of themselves or by comparison with the nations around them. And the wall is badly crooked. Isaiah uses the same picture: I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line (Isa 28:17).

I will never again pass by them means that God will no longer overlook their sins. This time Amos does not pray. The measurement has been taken, and there is nothing to say. There comes a point when a people's sin is so settled that God's patience ends.

What is God's plumb line for us? It is his law, and above all it is Jesus Christ himself, the only perfectly upright life ever lived. Measured against him, every one of us is crooked. That is why we need not only a plumb line but a Saviour. The One who measures us is the One who died for crooked people and makes them new.

the high places of Isaac shall be made desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste, and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword."

Judgment will fall on Israel's religion and its royal family. The high places and sanctuaries where Israel worshipped would be ruined. Isaac is used here as another name for the nation, the descendants of Isaac. And God will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. This came true when Jeroboam's son Zechariah reigned only six months before he was assassinated (2 Kgs 15:8-10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amaziah the priest of Bethel reports Amos to the king as a traitor (vv. 10-11) and orders him, never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary (vv. 12-13). Amos replies that he was no professional prophet: the LORD took me from following the flock and sent him (vv. 14-15). Because Amaziah tried to silence God's word, judgment will fall on his own family, and Israel will go into exile (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: No human authority can silence the word of God, and those who oppose it bring judgment on themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, "Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land is not able to bear all his words. For thus Amos has said, "'Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel must go into exile away from his land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, "Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land is not able to bear all his words.

Suddenly the book moves from visions to a real confrontation. Amaziah was the chief priest at Bethel, the royal shrine. He reports Amos to the king as a traitor: Amos has conspired against you. Amos was not plotting a rebellion. He was preaching God's word. But to a religious leader who served the government, a prophet who criticised the king looked like a political threat.

The land is not able to bear all his words. Amaziah is right in a way he did not intend. God's word was too heavy for a nation built on injustice. The same fear moved the religious leaders against Jesus: If we let him go on like this ... the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation (John 11:48).

For thus Amos has said, "'Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel must go into exile away from his land.'"

Amaziah's report twists Amos's words slightly. Amos said God would rise against the house of Jeroboam (v. 9), meaning his dynasty. Amaziah makes it sound like a personal threat against the king. In fact Jeroboam himself died in peace (2 Kgs 14:29), and it was his son who was killed. Notice also what Amaziah leaves out: the visions, the call to repentance and Amos's prayers for the people. Opponents of God's word often quote it selectively to make it sound as bad as possible.

verseByVerse.quote: And Amaziah said to Amos, "O seer, go, flee away to the land of Judah, and eat bread there, and prophesy there, but never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary, and it is a temple of the kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Amaziah said to Amos, "O seer, go, flee away to the land of Judah, and eat bread there, and prophesy there,

We are not told how the king replied. But Amaziah confronts Amos directly. O seer may be a sneer. Go, flee away to the land of Judah: go back where you came from. Eat bread there: earn your living there. Amaziah assumes that Amos is a religious professional preaching for money, just as Amaziah served the king for his living. He cannot imagine a man who speaks simply because God has sent him.

but never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary, and it is a temple of the kingdom."

Here is the real issue. Bethel was the king's sanctuary and a temple of the kingdom. Amaziah does not call it God's house. Religion had become a department of the state, there to support the king's power and bless the nation's success. In such a place, a prophet who speaks against the king has no place.

Churches can fall into the same trap whenever they become chaplains to political power, of any party, or when they want preaching that is comfortable and never challenges. Paul warned of people who will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim 4:3). The church belongs to Christ, not to any king or nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amos answered and said to Amaziah, "I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but I was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs. But the LORD took me from following the flock, and the LORD said to me, 'Go, prophesy to my people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Amos answered and said to Amaziah, "I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but I was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs.

Amos is not intimidated. I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son. (The ESV notes that it may be read "I am no prophet".) He is not denying that God has made him speak for him. He means he was not a professional prophet and did not belong to a group of trained prophets, such as the sons of the prophets found at Bethel in Elisha's day (2 Kgs 2:3). He did not choose this work to make a living. He had a job already. He was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs, which probably involved tending the fruit of a kind of fig tree so that it would ripen. It was humble farm work.

But the LORD took me from following the flock, and the LORD said to me, 'Go, prophesy to my people Israel.'

Here is Amos's authority: the LORD took me. He did not seek the role; God interrupted his life. God said almost the same thing to David: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep (2 Sam 7:8). And God called Israel my people. Amaziah called Bethel the king's temple, but Israel belonged to God, and God had the right to speak to them.

God still delights to use ordinary people. Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise (1 Cor 1:26-27). What matters is not our credentials but God's call. And when human authorities order God's servants to be quiet, the answer of the apostles still stands: We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore hear the word of the LORD. "You say, 'Do not prophesy against Israel, and do not preach against the house of Isaac.' Therefore thus says the LORD: "'Your wife shall be a prostitute in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be divided up with a measuring line; you yourself shall die in an unclean land, and Israel shall surely go into exile away from its land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now therefore hear the word of the LORD. "You say, 'Do not prophesy against Israel, and do not preach against the house of Isaac.'

Amaziah had told Amos to stop speaking. Amos answers by speaking again: hear the word of the LORD. He quotes Amaziah's own order back to him. The priest thought he could silence God. Instead, God's word now falls directly on him.

Therefore thus says the LORD: "'Your wife shall be a prostitute in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be divided up with a measuring line; you yourself shall die in an unclean land, and Israel shall surely go into exile away from its land.'"

These are terrible words, and they describe what happens when a city is conquered. Amaziah's wife would be left destitute, forced into prostitution to survive or abused by the invaders. His children would be killed. His land would be measured out and given to foreigners. And he himself, a priest who prided himself on ritual purity, would die in an unclean land, a pagan country far from home. The exile that Amaziah had tried to stop Amos from announcing would happen anyway. Israel shall surely go into exile. And it did: So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria (2 Kgs 17:23).

This is not Amos taking personal revenge. It is God's judgment on a religious leader who used his position to shut God's mouth. Those who hold spiritual office carry a heavy responsibility. But the warning is for everyone. Each of us can respond to God's word like Amaziah, telling it to go away, or like Amos, who heard it, prayed and obeyed. If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Gal 1:10).

7.title: The Plumb Line
7.overview:
God shows Amos a swarm of locusts forming as the latter growth sprouts after the king's mowings. When they have eaten the grass, Amos pleads, "O Lord GOD, please forgive! How can Jacob stand? He is so small!" and the LORD relents (vv. 1-3). God then shows a judgment by fire that devours the great deep and begins to eat up the land; Amos begs God to cease, and again the LORD relents (vv. 4-6).

In the third vision the Lord stands beside a wall built with a plumb line, holding a plumb line. He sets it in the midst of his people Israel and will never again pass by them: the high places of Isaac and the sanctuaries of Israel will be laid waste, and he will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword (vv. 7-9).

Amaziah the priest of Bethel reports to King Jeroboam that Amos has conspired against him, saying that Jeroboam will die by the sword and Israel go into exile. He orders Amos to flee to Judah, earn his bread there and never again prophesy at Bethel, the king's sanctuary (vv. 10-13). Amos answers that he was no prophet or prophet's son, but a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs whom the LORD took from following the flock and sent to prophesy to his people Israel (vv. 14-15). Because Amaziah forbids him to prophesy, his wife will become a prostitute in the city, his children will fall by the sword, his land will be divided, he will die in an unclean land, and Israel will surely go into exile (vv. 16-17).
7.theology:
God reveals his coming judgments so that his servants may pray and his people may repent (vv. 1, 4, 7; 3:7).

God hears the intercession of his people and has ordained prayer as a means of carrying out his unchanging purposes (vv. 2-3, 5-6; Exod 32:14; Num 23:19; Jas 5:16).

Christ is the perfect Intercessor, who not only pleads for his people but bears their judgment (vv. 2, 5; Heb 7:25; Rom 8:34).

God measures his people by his own standard, and his patience has a limit (vv. 7-9; Isa 28:17).

Religion that serves political power rather than God will oppose God's word (vv. 10-13; John 11:48; 2 Tim 4:3-4).

God's call, not human credentials, gives authority to speak his word, and his servants must obey God rather than men (vv. 14-15; 2 Sam 7:8; 1 Cor 1:26-27; Acts 4:19-20; 5:29).

Those who try to silence God's word bring judgment on themselves, and his word will be fulfilled (vv. 16-17; 2 Kgs 15:8-10; 17:23).
7.examples:
Locusts devouring the only grass left after the king has taken his share.

A prophet begging mercy for the people who despise him.

A fire so hot it dries up the waters under the earth.

A builder's string hanging straight beside a leaning wall.

A priest reporting a preacher to the king as a traitor.

A farmhand telling the chief priest that God took him from the flock.

A temple called the king's sanctuary instead of God's house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — A Basket of Summer Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows Amos a basket of summer fruit and says, The end has come upon my people Israel; I will never again pass by them (vv. 1-2). The songs of the temple will turn to wailing over the dead (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel is ripe for judgment, and the end is at hand.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, a basket of summer fruit. And he said, "Amos, what do you see?" And I said, "A basket of summer fruit." Then the LORD said to me, "The end has come upon my people Israel; I will never again pass by them. The songs of the temple shall become wailings in that day," declares the Lord GOD. "So many dead bodies!" "They are thrown everywhere!" "Silence!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, a basket of summer fruit.

And he said, "Amos, what do you see?" And I said, "A basket of summer fruit." Then the LORD said to me, "The end has come upon my people Israel; I will never again pass by them.

The fourth vision looks harmless: a basket of summer fruit, the ripe figs and other fruit picked at the end of the harvest season. But the meaning lies in the sound of the words. As the ESV notes, the Hebrew words for summer fruit and end sound alike (qayits and qets). God points to the ripe fruit and says, The end has come. Like fruit at the end of summer, Israel is ripe. It is ready for harvest, and soon it will begin to rot.

As in the plumb line vision, Amos asks for no mercy, and God repeats, I will never again pass by them (7:8). The time for warnings is ending.

The songs of the temple shall become wailings in that day," declares the Lord GOD. "So many dead bodies!" "They are thrown everywhere!" "Silence!"

The joyful songs of the temple (the ESV notes this may be "palace", and may mean the singing women of the palace) will turn into wailings. The last words come in short, broken cries, like a survivor walking through a ruined city: So many dead bodies! They are thrown everywhere! Silence! There are too many dead to bury properly, and grief leaves people speechless (compare 6:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The merchants who trample on the needy cannot wait for the holy days to end so they can cheat with false scales and buy the poor for silver (vv. 4-6). God swears, Surely I will never forget any of their deeds (v. 7). The land will heave like the Nile (v. 8), the sun will go down at noon, and the feasts will become mourning like the mourning for an only son (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: God remembers every act of dishonesty against the poor, and he will turn the joy of the oppressor into grief.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, you who trample on the needy and bring the poor of the land to an end, saying, "When will the new moon be over, that we may sell grain? And the Sabbath, that we may offer wheat for sale, that we may make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances, that we may buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals and sell the chaff of the wheat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this, you who trample on the needy and bring the poor of the land to an end,

Why is Israel ripe for judgment? Amos returns to the sin he has exposed from the beginning (2:6-8). The powerful trample on the needy, and they aim to bring the poor ... to an end, pushing them off their land and out of existence.

saying, "When will the new moon be over, that we may sell grain? And the Sabbath, that we may offer wheat for sale, that we may make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances,

Amos lets us overhear the merchants. They kept the religious holidays. They closed their shops on the new moon festival at the start of each month (Num 10:10) and on the Sabbath. But their hearts were in the marketplace. They sat through worship thinking, "When will this be over, so I can get back to making money?"

And they cheated. An ephah was a measure for grain (about 22 liters, as the ESV notes), and a shekel was a weight used to weigh silver (about 11 grams). The merchants made the ephah small, so the buyer got less grain, and the shekel great, so he paid more silver. They tipped the scales both ways. God's law demanded just balances, just weights, a just ephah (Lev 19:36). A false balance is an abomination to the LORD (Prov 11:1).

that we may buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals and sell the chaff of the wheat?"

The poor, cheated until they fell into debt, were then bought as slaves for silver or for the price of a pair of sandals (2:6). Meanwhile the merchants sold the chaff of the wheat, the sweepings from the threshing floor, mixed in with the grain. They made a profit even from rubbish.

This is a portrait of a divided heart: religious on the holy day, ruthless on the business day. Jesus said, You cannot serve God and money (Luke 16:13). How we treat customers, employees and those who owe us money is as much a matter of worship as how we sing on Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has sworn by the pride of Jacob: "Surely I will never forget any of their deeds. Shall not the land tremble on this account, and everyone mourn who dwells in it, and all of it rise like the Nile, and be tossed about and sink again, like the Nile of Egypt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has sworn by the pride of Jacob: "Surely I will never forget any of their deeds.

God takes an oath. What does he swear by? The pride of Jacob may be said with irony: God swears by Israel's arrogance, which is as fixed and unchanging as God himself (compare 6:8). Or it may be a title for God himself, who is Jacob's true pride, much as Samuel calls God the Glory of Israel (1 Sam 15:29). Either way, the oath is solemn: Surely I will never forget any of their deeds. The merchants thought no one noticed their small cheats. God keeps every record.

That is a terrifying thought for anyone outside Christ. It is also a great comfort for the poor who have been cheated. And for those who trust in Christ, God makes an astonishing promise: I will remember their sins no more, because Christ has borne them (Heb 8:12).

Shall not the land tremble on this account, and everyone mourn who dwells in it, and all of it rise like the Nile, and be tossed about and sink again, like the Nile of Egypt?"

Sin shakes the earth. The whole land will tremble, rising and sinking like the Nile river in Egypt, which rose every year in flood and then fell again. This may picture a great earthquake, like the one mentioned at the start of the book (1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "And on that day," declares the Lord GOD, "I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight. I will turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation; I will bring sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make it like the mourning for an only son and the end of it like a bitter day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And on that day," declares the Lord GOD, "I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight.

On that day, the day of the LORD, the sun will set at noon. Darkness in the middle of the day is a sign that everything is turned upside down. The day of the LORD is darkness, and not light (5:18).

I will turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation; I will bring sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make it like the mourning for an only son and the end of it like a bitter day.

The feasts where the merchants celebrated their profits will become funerals. People will wear sackcloth, rough cloth worn in grief, and shave their heads, a sign of mourning. The deepest grief of all is the mourning for an only son, when parents lose their only child and with him their future.

These words find a deeper echo in the Gospels. When the only Son of God hung on the cross, there was darkness over the whole land from about noon until the ninth hour, while the sun's light failed (Luke 23:44-45). Zechariah foretold that people would look on the one they pierced and mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child (Zech 12:10). God did not spare his only Son (John 3:16). The darkness of judgment fell on him so that it need not fall on us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Not a Famine of Bread
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will send a famine on the land— not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD (v. 11). People will search from sea to sea and not find it (v. 12). Young people will faint, and those who swear by false gods shall fall, and never rise again (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The worst judgment is for God to fall silent to those who would not listen.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming," declares the Lord GOD, "when I will send a famine on the land— not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD. They shall wander from sea to sea, and from north to east; they shall run to and fro, to seek the word of the LORD, but they shall not find it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the days are coming," declares the Lord GOD, "when I will send a famine on the land— not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD.

Israel had known famine and drought (4:6-8). Now God warns of something worse: a famine ... of hearing the words of the LORD. Israel had told the prophets to be quiet (2:12), and Amaziah had ordered Amos away from Bethel (7:12-13). God will give them what they asked for. He will stop speaking. When people refuse God's word long enough, he may take it away. There was a time like this in Israel's history already, when the word of the LORD was rare in those days (1 Sam 3:1).

They shall wander from sea to sea, and from north to east; they shall run to and fro, to seek the word of the LORD, but they shall not find it.

When disaster comes, people will desperately want a word from God. They will wander everywhere, from sea to sea, searching for a prophet. But they shall not find it. God had warned in Proverbs, they will seek me diligently but will not find me (Prov 1:28). They wanted God's word only when it was too late.

This is a sober warning for a world full of Bibles. It is possible to have God's word close at hand and never truly hear it, until the heart grows so hard that it cannot hear at all. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb 3:15). Jesus said, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt 4:4). And Jesus himself is God's final Word. When many turned away, Peter said, Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life (John 6:68).

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day the lovely virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst. Those who swear by the Guilt of Samaria, and say, 'As your god lives, O Dan,' and, 'As the Way of Beersheba lives,' they shall fall, and never rise again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the lovely virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst.

Even the young men and lovely virgins, the strongest and most beautiful of the nation, will faint for thirst. The thirst is physical, but it also pictures the spiritual famine of verse 11. A generation cut off from God's word withers.

Those who swear by the Guilt of Samaria, and say, 'As your god lives, O Dan,' and, 'As the Way of Beersheba lives,' they shall fall, and never rise again."

Why will they faint? Because they have drunk from false wells. They swear oaths by false gods: the Guilt of Samaria, some idol worshipped in the capital; the god of Dan, where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf (2 Kgs 10:29); and the Way of Beersheba, the pilgrimage road to the southern shrine (5:5). To swear by something is to trust it. They trusted their idols and their pilgrimages. They shall fall, and never rise again, the same words Amos used in his funeral song for Israel (5:2). Only the living God can give water that satisfies (John 4:14).

8.title: A Famine of the Word
8.overview:
God shows Amos a basket of summer fruit and declares that the end has come upon his people Israel; he will never again pass by them. The songs of the temple will become wailing, and dead bodies will be thrown everywhere in silence (vv. 1-3).

Amos addresses those who trample the needy, who cannot wait for the new moon and Sabbath to end so they can sell grain with a small ephah, a heavy shekel and false balances, buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, and sell the chaff with the wheat (vv. 4-6). The LORD swears by the pride of Jacob that he will never forget their deeds. The land will tremble and heave like the Nile (vv. 7-8). On that day the sun will go down at noon, feasts will turn to mourning, sackcloth and baldness will be everywhere, like the mourning for an only son (vv. 9-10).

Days are coming when God will send a famine, not of bread or water, but of hearing the words of the LORD. People will wander from sea to sea seeking his word and not find it (vv. 11-12). The young will faint for thirst, and those who swear by the Guilt of Samaria, the god of Dan and the Way of Beersheba will fall and never rise again (vv. 13-14).
8.theology:
There comes a time when a people is ripe for judgment and God's patience ends (vv. 1-3; 7:8).

Religious observance combined with dishonesty in business is hateful to God; he demands just weights and fair dealing (vv. 4-6; Lev 19:35-36; Prov 11:1; Luke 16:13).

God never forgets the deeds of the unrepentant, yet in Christ he remembers his people's sins no more (v. 7; Heb 8:12).

The day of the LORD turns celebration into mourning; its darkness fell on Christ, God's only Son, at the cross (vv. 9-10; Luke 23:44-45; Zech 12:10; John 3:16).

God's word is life, and to lose it is a worse famine than lack of bread; those who reject it may find it withdrawn (vv. 11-12; 1 Sam 3:1; Prov 1:28; Matt 4:4; Heb 3:15).

Trusting in idols and religious routes leads to a fall with no recovery; only Christ has the words of eternal life (vv. 13-14; John 6:68).
8.examples:
A basket of ripe figs that means the end has come.

A merchant counting the hours until the Sabbath is over.

A scale weighted one way for grain and the other way for silver.

Chaff swept up from the floor and sold as wheat.

The sun going down at noon on a feast day.

People running from sea to sea looking for a word from God.
