verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — No Escape and a Sifting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amos sees the Lord standing beside the altar, commanding it to be struck down (v. 1). No one can escape, whether in Sheol, heaven, on Carmel or at the bottom of the sea (vv. 2-4), for he is the Lord of all creation (vv. 5-6). Israel's exodus does not make them untouchable (v. 7). God will destroy the sinful kingdom, except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob (v. 8). He will shake Israel as one shakes with a sieve, and the sinners who say disaster will not overtake them will die (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: No one can hide from God's judgment, yet in judgment he preserves a remnant for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and he said: "Strike the capitals until the thresholds shake, and shatter them on the heads of all the people; and those who are left of them I will kill with the sword; not one of them shall flee away; not one of them shall escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and he said: "Strike the capitals until the thresholds shake, and shatter them on the heads of all the people; and those who are left of them I will kill with the sword; not one of them shall flee away; not one of them shall escape.

The fifth and final vision is different. There is no question, "Amos, what do you see?", and no prayer. Amos simply sees the Lord standing beside the altar (the ESV notes it may be "on" the altar). This was probably the altar at Bethel, the heart of Israel's false worship. People went there to seek protection from God. Now God himself stands there, not to receive their sacrifices but to judge.

He commands, Strike the capitals, the decorated tops of the pillars that held up the roof, until the thresholds shake, so that the whole building shudders from top to bottom. The temple will collapse on the heads of all the people (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads "all of them"). Those who survive will be killed as they flee: not one of them shall escape. The religion Israel trusted in became the place of its destruction. Religion without repentance is no refuge from God.

verseByVerse.quote: "If they dig into Sheol, from there shall my hand take them; if they climb up to heaven, from there I will bring them down. If they hide themselves on the top of Carmel, from there I will search them out and take them; and if they hide from my sight at the bottom of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it shall bite them. And if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it shall kill them; and I will fix my eyes upon them for evil and not for good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"If they dig into Sheol, from there shall my hand take them; if they climb up to heaven, from there I will bring them down.

If they hide themselves on the top of Carmel, from there I will search them out and take them; and if they hide from my sight at the bottom of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it shall bite them.

And if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it shall kill them; and I will fix my eyes upon them for evil and not for good."

Imagine trying to hide from God. Go down to Sheol, the realm of the dead deep below. God's hand will reach there. Climb up to heaven, and he will bring you down. Hide in the thick forests and caves on the top of Carmel, and he will search you out. Hide at the bottom of the sea, and he will command the serpent of the deep to find you. Even in exile, far from home, his sword will follow.

These verses sound like Psalm 139: If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! (Ps 139:8). But the tone is the opposite. For the psalmist, God's presence everywhere is a comfort: even there your hand shall lead me (Ps 139:10). For those who are running from God in rebellion, the same truth is a terror. The difference is not in God but in us. No creature is hidden from his sight (Heb 4:13).

The saddest words are these: I will fix my eyes upon them for evil and not for good. Normally, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him (Ps 33:18), to protect them. Here his eyes are fixed on Israel for judgment. There is only one place to hide from the judgment of God, and that is in God himself, through Christ, who bore it for us.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD of hosts, he who touches the earth and it melts, and all who dwell in it mourn, and all of it rises like the Nile, and sinks again, like the Nile of Egypt; who builds his upper chambers in the heavens and founds his vault upon the earth; who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the surface of the earth— the LORD is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord GOD of hosts, he who touches the earth and it melts, and all who dwell in it mourn, and all of it rises like the Nile, and sinks again, like the Nile of Egypt;

For the third time Amos breaks into a hymn (compare 4:13; 5:8-9). Who is this God who searches out the hiding places? His power is overwhelming. He only has to touch the earth, and it melts. The land heaves up and down like the Nile in flood (compare 8:8). The mountains and fortresses Israel trusted in are like wax before him.

who builds his upper chambers in the heavens and founds his vault upon the earth; who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the surface of the earth— the LORD is his name.

God's dwelling is not a shrine at Bethel. He builds his upper chambers in the heavens and rules the waters of the sea (5:8). This is the God Israel had tried to keep in a box. He cannot be managed, bribed or hidden from, yet he has made himself known in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you not like the Cushites to me, O people of Israel?" declares the LORD. "Did I not bring up Israel from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir? Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the surface of the ground, except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Are you not like the Cushites to me, O people of Israel?" declares the LORD. "Did I not bring up Israel from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir?

This verse would have shocked Israel. The Cushites lived far to the south, along the upper Nile beyond Egypt. To Israel they were a distant, foreign people. God says, Are you not like the Cushites to me? Israel thought the exodus made them untouchable. Yes, God brought Israel out of Egypt. But he also directed the movements of other nations. He brought the Philistines from Caphtor (probably the island of Crete; compare Deut 2:23) and the Syrians from Kir (compare 1:5).

The exodus was never a guarantee that Israel could sin without consequence. A people who forget God's grace and live like the nations will be treated like the nations. God rules all history: he made from one man every nation of mankind and determined the boundaries of their dwelling place (Acts 17:26). There is also a hidden hint of hope here. The God who cares about Cushites and Philistines will one day gather people from every nation (v. 12).

Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the surface of the ground, except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob," declares the LORD.

God's eyes are on the sinful kingdom, the nation of Israel as a political power, and he will wipe it out. And he did; the northern kingdom never returned. But then comes the word that changes everything: except. I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob. God's covenant promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will not fail. The kingdom will fall, but the people of God will not come to an end. This is the turning point of the whole book.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, I will command, and shake the house of Israel among all the nations as one shakes with a sieve, but no pebble shall fall to the earth. All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, who say, 'Disaster shall not overtake or meet us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For behold, I will command, and shake the house of Israel among all the nations as one shakes with a sieve, but no pebble shall fall to the earth.

How can God both destroy and preserve? The answer is a sieve. When grain was sifted, the good grain and the stones and rubbish were separated by shaking. Scholars differ on exactly how this sieve worked, whether it held back the pebbles or let the grain through. But the point is clear. God will shake Israel among all the nations in exile, and his sifting will be precise. No pebble shall fall to the earth: nothing will slip through by accident. No sinner will escape, and not one of God's own will be lost.

This is deeply comforting for Christians in hard times. Jesus told Peter, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31-32). Trials shake us, but they cannot shake a true believer out of God's hand. No one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, who say, 'Disaster shall not overtake or meet us.'

Who will be caught in the sieve? The sinners of my people, those who say, Disaster shall not overtake or meet us. Their sin is not only what they did but the false confidence with which they did it. They did not believe God's warnings. Being among God's people outwardly saves no one who persists in unbelief.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–15 — I Will Raise Up the Booth of David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that all the nations who are called by my name will belong to it (vv. 11-12). The harvest will be so rich that the plowman shall overtake the reaper (v. 13). God will restore his people; they will rebuild, plant and eat, and they shall never again be uprooted (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's last word is grace: through the Son of David he gathers a people from all nations into a kingdom that will never end.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old, that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name," declares the LORD who does this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old,

Suddenly, after chapter upon chapter of judgment, the sun breaks through. In that day, the day of the LORD, which was darkness for the rebellious, becomes a day of restoration. God will raise up the booth of David that is fallen.

A booth was a simple shelter made of branches, the kind of temporary hut used at harvest time. The picture is humbling. David's great royal house, his dynasty, would be so broken that it would look like a flimsy hut collapsing in a field. And that is what happened: Judah's kings were carried into exile, and no son of David sat on a throne. But God promises to raise up David's fallen house, repair its breaches and rebuild it as in the days of old, like the glorious days of David himself.

This promise was fulfilled in Jesus Christ. The angel told Mary, the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever (Luke 1:32-33). Peter preached that David foresaw the resurrection of the Christ, the descendant God had sworn to set on his throne (Acts 2:30-31). When God raised Jesus from the dead and seated him at his right hand, he raised up the fallen house of David. Jesus calls himself the root and the descendant of David (Rev 22:16).

that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name," declares the LORD who does this.

The restored kingdom of David will include the remnant of Edom, Israel's old enemy (1:11), and all the nations who are called by my name. To be called by God's name means to belong to him (Deut 28:10). David had once ruled over surrounding nations by conquest. The greater Son of David would gather the nations to belong to God.

The apostles understood this verse in exactly this way. At the council in Jerusalem, when the church had to decide whether Gentiles must become Jews to follow Christ, James quoted Amos: I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen, that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name (Acts 15:16-17). James's wording is different because he quotes the Greek translation of the Old Testament (as the ESV notes). The Greek reads the remnant of mankind where the Hebrew has the remnant of Edom. But the meaning is the same: the nations, even Israel's enemies, will be brought under the rule of David's Son. James saw it happening as Gentiles believed in Jesus.

Christians understand the full fulfilment of this promise in different ways. Many in the Reformed tradition believe that Acts 15 shows the promise being fulfilled now: Christ reigns as David's Son, and the Gentiles coming into the church are the nations called by God's name. Many dispensational Christians agree that Acts 15 shows the church in harmony with this prophecy, but believe its complete fulfilment awaits a future earthly kingdom when Christ reigns from Jerusalem. All agree that Jesus is the promised Son of David, gathering people from every nation. Gentile believers who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming," declares the LORD, "when the plowman shall overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes him who sows the seed; the mountains shall drip sweet wine, and all the hills shall flow with it. I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel, and they shall rebuild the ruined cities and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and drink their wine, and they shall make gardens and eat their fruit. I will plant them on their land, and they shall never again be uprooted out of the land that I have given them," says the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the days are coming," declares the LORD, "when the plowman shall overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes him who sows the seed; the mountains shall drip sweet wine, and all the hills shall flow with it.

The book that began with pastures withering (1:2) ends with a picture of overflowing abundance. Normally grain was harvested in spring, grapes trodden in late summer, and fields plowed and sown in the autumn. Now the harvest will be so enormous that the reapers are still at work when the plowman arrives for the next crop. God's law had promised such blessing for obedience (Lev 26:5). The mountains shall drip sweet wine, as Joel also foresaw (Joel 3:18). Locusts, drought and blight (4:6-11) are replaced by endless plenty.

I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel, and they shall rebuild the ruined cities and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and drink their wine, and they shall make gardens and eat their fruit.

Every curse is reversed. Earlier God had said, you have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine (5:11). Now they shall plant vineyards and drink their wine. The ruined cities will be rebuilt and lived in. What sin destroyed, grace restores, as in Isaiah's picture of the new creation: They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit (Isa 65:21).

I will plant them on their land, and they shall never again be uprooted out of the land that I have given them," says the LORD your God.

God himself will plant his people like a tree, and they shall never again be uprooted. The exile will not have the last word. And notice the final words: the LORD your God. After all the judgment, God still calls himself your God. The covenant stands.

How will this be fulfilled? Some Christians believe it promises a literal future restoration of the Jewish people to the land of Israel in a coming earthly kingdom. Many in the Reformed tradition believe that the promise of land is fulfilled and enlarged in Christ: Abraham was promised that he would be heir of the world (Rom 4:13), and God's people look for a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Heb 11:16), the new heavens and new earth, where no one will ever be uprooted again. Many Reformed Christians also believe, from Romans 11, that there will be a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end (Rom 11:25-26). Whatever our view of the details, God's final word to his people is not judgment but home.

Amos began with a lion's roar. He ends with a harvest that never stops. Between the two stands the Son of David, who took the roar of judgment on himself at the cross and rose to rule forever. In him, God's people will be planted in a new creation, and the dwelling place of God is with man (Rev 21:3).

9.title: The Booth of David
9.overview:
Amos sees the Lord standing beside the altar, commanding the capitals to be struck so that the temple collapses on the people, and those who flee will be killed; not one will escape (v. 1). Whether they dig into Sheol, climb to heaven, hide on Carmel or at the bottom of the sea, or go into captivity, God will find them and fix his eyes on them for evil (vv. 2-4). He is the Lord GOD of hosts, who touches the earth and it melts, builds his chambers in the heavens and pours out the sea on the earth (vv. 5-6).

Israel is no different to God from the Cushites; he brought Israel from Egypt, but also the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir. His eyes are on the sinful kingdom, and he will destroy it, except that he will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob (vv. 7-8). He will shake Israel among the nations as with a sieve, and no pebble will fall to the earth, while all the sinners who say disaster will not overtake them will die by the sword (vv. 9-10).

In that day God will raise up the fallen booth of David, repair its breaches and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations called by his name (vv. 11-12). The days are coming when the plowman will overtake the reaper and the mountains will drip sweet wine. God will restore the fortunes of his people; they will rebuild the ruined cities, plant vineyards and drink their wine, and he will plant them on their land, never again to be uprooted (vv. 13-15).
9.theology:
No one can escape God's judgment, and false worship becomes the place where it falls (vv. 1-4; Heb 4:13).

God's presence everywhere is terror to the rebel and comfort to the one who trusts him (vv. 2-4; Ps 139:7-10; Ps 33:18).

God rules the history of all nations, and past privilege gives no licence to sin (v. 7; Acts 17:26).

In judgment God preserves a remnant, and none of his own will be lost (vv. 8-9; Luke 22:31-32; John 10:27-29).

God keeps his promise to David by raising up Jesus Christ, David's Son, to reign forever (v. 11; Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:30-31; Rev 22:16).

The kingdom of David's Son includes people from all nations, as the apostles recognised in the inclusion of the Gentiles (v. 12; Acts 15:13-18; Eph 2:12-13; Rev 7:9).

God's final word to his people is restoration: every curse reversed and a home from which they will never be uprooted, fulfilled in the new creation (vv. 13-15; Lev 26:5; Isa 65:21-22; Rom 4:13; Heb 11:16; Rev 21:3-4).
9.examples:
A temple collapsing on the worshippers who trusted in it.

A fugitive hiding at the bottom of the sea, and God finding him there.

A sieve shaken hard, and not one grain lost.

A collapsed shelter in a field, rebuilt into a royal house.

A council in Jerusalem reading Amos as Gentiles come to faith.

A harvest so large the plowman catches up with the reapers.

Vineyards planted, and this time the planters drink the wine.
